RADAR WARNING LINES
speechtext: Arising out of the action of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in tabling these agreements between the United States and Canada, is the minister in a position to advise what is Canada's proportionate share of the cost, in respect of the distant early warning line, the mid-continent line and the "Pinetree" line? What is Canada's proportion of the expenditures being made, and in the construction work done by the United States to what degree is Canadian sovereignty maintained?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RADAR WARNING LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not in a position to give the exact proportions of cost borne by the two countries in respect of the three lines, because the total cost has not yet been determined. However, I might make a short statement on the point raised by my hon. friend in the last part of his question.
Hon. members will recall that the statement on the over-all joint Canada-United States warning system, published as appendix B to Hansard of February 22, 1955, emphasized that experience has shown that projects of this nature can be carried out most effectively by vesting responsibility for all phases of the work of construction and installation in a single authority. Accordingly it had been agreed that Canada would construct the mid-Canada warning line and the United States the distant early warning line.
3956	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry
This exchange of notes establishes conditions which will enable the United States to build the distant early warning line as rapidly as possible in the interests of the defence of the two countries. At the same time it preserves the principle enunciated in the joint declaration of February 12, 1947, on defence co-operation, that all co-operative arrangements will be without impairment of the control of either country over all activities in its own territory. In particular the agreement provides for the effective participation by Canada in the operation of the distant early warning system, the character of such participation to be determined on the basis of studies to be carried out during the construction phase. These studies are already under way, but I should point out that they will not be completed for a considerable time and for the present there is nothing to be added to the statement made by the Prime Minister on the matter in this house on February 22 last.

speechtext: When the committee rose last evening we were discussing resolution 173. Shall the resolution carry?

Mr. Chairman, before this
resolution is carried I have just a few remarks to make concerning the debate of yesterday. It is not often that a cabinet minister is described by members of the opposition as being sympathetic. That fine word was used yesterday with reference to the Minister of Labour. The greatest tribute paid to him by hon. members who engaged in the discussion was the friendliness of that discussion. For the first time during the session the matter of unemployment was considered objectively, with a view to bringing relief to the unemployed. I am not going to refer to all the speeches that were made, but all members seemed to be in good disposition and made many useful suggestions for the improvement of labour conditions throughout the country.
I believe the real advisory council and the real board of inquiry is just this House of Commons. Hon. members belonging to all parties, who are familiar with conditions in their own constituencies and in the country at large, are in a much better position to offer suggestions and perhaps are better qualified than supposed economic experts or even

judges. I sympathize with the minister because so many suggestions have been made, and naturally he must make a choice. That will take a little time, because the more suggestions that are made, the more time it will take to make a selection.
The hon. lady member for Hamilton West suggested that the advisory council should resume its activities. Then the Leader of the Opposition followed her and suggested that a board of inquiry should be set up. The two suggestions are entirely different. I was surprised to hear one suggestion being made by the labour expert of the official opposition and the other by the Leader of the Opposition himself. They should discuss things together before making such pronouncements, in order to present a united front to the House of Commons.
I have always advocated that members of parliament should have the widest possible opportunities not only to make suggestions but to make recommendations to the government. This can be done in many ways, but it can be done particularly at the meetings of the industrial relations committee, where members of all parties gather to study labour problems and the labour situation at large.
Besides what may be said to him by members of the House of Commons, the minister has the advantage of having an organization in his own department dealing with these matters. I refer to the unemployment insurance commission, which has offices spread right across the country. They report not only on unemployment but also on employment. My personal experience, and this must be the experience of my colleagues, has been that the work done by the employment offices is most useful, not only to the government because of the information conveyed to them but mainly to those who are without work and who obtain employment through the services of the employment branch of the unemployment insurance commission.
Some years ago those engaged in lumbering did not come under the unemployment insurance commission. Some hon. members, and I was one of the first to join with them, insisted that these men should enjoy the benefits of the Unemployment Insurance Act. It has worked out that way. The former minister of labour listened to our requests and made a favourable decision; therefore in my constituency there are many people who enjoy the benefits of the Unemployment Insurance Act when they are engaged in the lumbering business.
It is precisely on account of that fact that the number of unemployed has increased. It is to be regretted, of course, but it is due to the seasonal nature of the occupation, and
Supply-Labour
those men, with their families, are very fortunate in getting the benefits of the Unemployment Insurance Act when they are out of work. I am most appreciative of what is done by the Minister of Labour for them.
Along with other members I have the responsibility of dealing with quite a large correspondence. When those men expect an answer from the unemployment insurance commission and it does not come as soon as they would like, they write their member of parliament in order that he may put pressure on the bureau to see that they get what is due them as soon as possible, because they are in great need. Then the member of parliament writes on their behalf to the unemployment insurance office, to the chief commissioner of the unemployment insurance commission, or to the minister, in order to give them satisfaction. It gives us an opportunity to familiarize ourselves with those problems. I do not complain about it, though it represents a good deal of work.
Without deprecating the speeches that were made by all the hon. members who spoke yesterday, I wish to say that the hon. gentleman who has put his finger on the spot is the hon. member for Cape Breton South. He said yesterday that unemployment was due in large measure to automation. He defined it, at page 3919 of yesterday's Hansard, as "the displacement of man by the machine". It is true. At the time we discussed the matter before the railway and shipping committee some years ago it was very unfortunate that some miners in Nova Scotia were deprived of work because of the dieselization of the Canadian National Railways. That was due to new machines.
At that time I joined the hon. member for Cape Breton South in protesting against that measure because I thought the old locomotives, which were good enough to haul large numbers of cars from coast to coast, were still of use, and it was important that they should burn coal in order to provide work for the miners of Nova Scotia, who deserve a lot of sympathy. But it was decided that the company had to go ahead with the times, that it was important to have diesel locomotives and to lay aside the good old iron horses that had done such a good job. This is one case where many good men of the railway were laid off. Some of them were transferred elsewhere, and some became unemployed.
There are many causes for unemployment. I do not intend to mention them all today. I mention only a few of which I have personal knowledge. For instance, in my county we have a branch of Canadian Arsenals Limited. Work there depends on the contracts that are

Supply-Labour
given to the company for the manufacture of munitions. When peace is advocated throughout the world it is only natural that the manufacture of munitions will decrease accordingly. We cannot have peace and war at the same time. Most of the munitions were sold to other countries, and when contracts expired it was only natural that the number of men employed should be reduced. It is very unfortunate, but this is the way it works. I understand quite well that it was not the fault of the government. There again I am in a difficult situation. I have explained it to the men, who understand it is much better to make progress toward peace than to have a war that would destroy homes and people and leave the country in a complete mess.
There is the question of good understanding between employer and employee. In that regard a very apt suggestion was made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, and I am the happier to mention it because he is not in the chamber at the present time. He suggested that industrial councils be established for various industries, in the same fashion as there are councils in the building trades.
This is a very good suggestion. The government cannot impose drastic conditions of employment on employers. It cannot be done. Employers must show good faith and a willingness to co-operate with the staff and personnel of their organizations. To me it was one of the ablest suggestions offered during the discussion yesterday. The same thing exists already in the building trades, and it is satisfactory. Why not use it in other industries?
It cannot be done tomorrow. It will take some time to do it. Persuasion must be used to make both parties understand the situation and finally come to an understanding that would be for the benefit of the country. But if employers were aroused against employees, if the employers were to believe that the employees' requests were extravagant, it could not work. I hope there will be good understanding between the employers and the employees in all branches of industry in this country. I am sure the best man to bring about such a happy conclusion is the Minister of Labour himself. He has done so much.
If we look at the estimates we see all the items that are mentioned under the Department of Labour. It is quite astounding to see all that is done by this department, ' including vocational training and all that sort of thing. I wish the minister good luck and I know the future will not be as dark

as it was painted at the beginning of the session, because there must be peace on earth to men of good will.

Most of the remarks on this first item, Mr. Chairman, have followed the general pattern of praise for the department in various degrees and then suggestions, also I suppose in various degrees. I should like to say that I personally recognize that the labour department has been going through rather strenuous times these last few years, with the unemployment situation as it is and with the increase in legislation that has been necessary. I feel that these extra duties are being handled in very fine fashion, and a word of praise from me along the lines I mentioned earlier is in order.
So far as suggestions go I have one personal gripe against the department, and if the few remarks I propose to make could be considered as suggestions I should like to just leave them with the house. I say there is a great tendency in Canada, on the part of the labour department and the other groups and associations who compile statistics of various kinds in connection with labour, to consider the over-all national picture too much and leave out the regional aspect. It is a recognized fact that unemployment is regional. There are many other phases that affect the labour department which have also been unanimously considered as regional. Naturally I have a personal gripe, in that the maritimes and the Atlantic regions, which have very particular and peculiar problems with respect to labour, are being ill-considered in this respect.
Having said that I believe we are getting away from the regional aspect to a certain extent in our consideration of labour and its problems in Canada, I should like to reflect on some of these small matters in the maritimes which I feel present a particular regional aspect as contrasted with any sort of national study that might be presented by the department and these other agencies.
First of all, I suggest that we have a particular problem of low wages in the maritimes. In a recent issue of the Financial Post figures were given showing wages in the construction industry and pointing out that they are climbing. The table setting out these figures is divided into the principal metropolitan areas in Canada, showing the various trades as well as unskilled labour. I am not going to put these figures on record because I am embarrassed by the low wages that are listed for Halifax and Saint John. If hon. members will just take my word for the fact that the figures are so low I am embarrassed to put them on the record, that will serve to illustrate my point.

Second, I should like to refer to the older citizens who are coming into a position of increasing importance in our life today. The problems of people over 45 who are attempting to obtain work are well known to everybody. The older people in the Atlantic region are a definite problem, even more than in the central region, because jobs for which they are fitted are not available. Such jobs as night watchman and other supervisory jobs are only connected with large industry and large buildings which, as a result of our small-scale economy, are not found in that region.
Third, I think the fishermen present a definite regional problem. They are now being considered for unemployment insurance. While I do not wish to go into that question, I feel that any arguments concerning the administrative difficulties that would prevent any sort of unemployment insurance being extended to these fishermen should not weigh too heavily. These fishermen will always be in small organizations, and they will be in various areas. There is no possible chance there will ever be a great concentration of them.
The coal industry of the maritimes is another industry that needs special consideration. It definitely presents a regional problem. I believe it is today that a meeting is taking place in Halifax, to which reference has already been made in this debate, in an attempt to alleviate this situation.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I want to refer to the general geographic conditions that would make the labour situation in the maritimes, and its interrelated fields, a special consideration. I would mention briefly the immobility of labour that exists down our way, and the difficulties that have to be considered in this respect. I refer also to the small markets that exist in this region, and the tremendous drawback that factor is to any attempts at manufacturing in that area.
Having said that we have these various regional problems, and having said that I feel the various people who compile labour statistics are not giving us adequate consideration from a strictly regional standpoint, I throw out these few suggestions to the department and other groups that may, in the future, compile such statistics.
First of all I feel that we always seem to wait too long before attempting to catch up with a problem. There are two very good examples of this in New Brunswick that are of recent date. I refer to the Marysville textile shut-down of two years ago, at which time we lost one of the main industries in
Supply-Labour
our community. When the mill was finally shut down, through the combined efforts of provincial, federal and local authorities it was possible to relocate most of the workers through a vocational training plan.
I feel that the situation in this case has been righted to some extent. But why was it that we had to wait until the thing had dragged on and dislocated so many people? Why could not plans have been made in advance to meet this special problem, a problem which was really unique, though I realize that other textile plants have been closed down in Canada. I doubt, however, if there have been many other cases in which a community has been dependent upon one mill.
I would refer also to the Milltown textile mill which, as hon. members may know, has been able to continue in the area due to some sort of unique co-operative plan. It has been another experiment, and I believe a fairly successful one. However, their production is not what it was.
The various co-operative measures of all authorities have been appreciated. I suggest that here are two regional matters that could have been dealt with, and concerning which plans could have been made. It was not necessary to wait until a difficult situation developed. Plans and research could have been carried out long ago to cope with these problems.
It would be interesting to have a statement from the Minister of Labour about these two matters when he sums up in closing the debate, because I think they are unique experiments in Canada and we could probably get some helpful information if we knew just what had been done. Incidentally, vocational training grants were very helpful in Marysville. We hope that any reduction in the estimates will not affect these regions in the Atlantic provinces, which depend so much upon assistance of this kind.
Then I would refer to the various articles, particularly those dealing with research, compiled by the Department of Labour. I have before me a most commendable article dealing with labour research to which reference has been made by other speakers. This is prepared by the Canadian Congress of Labour, and I seem to detect in it the hand of Mr. Forsey. It purports to be a survey of economic trends in the Atlantic provinces. This work is startling and revealing, and I suggest that perhaps officials in the Department of Labour might work along similar lines. It may be that they have done research work that is just as good, dealing with regional aspects of the matter, but I must say they have not come to my attention. I just mention this in a friendly way.

Supply-Labour
Then I noticed in the press a few days ago that on the occasion of his trip to Nova Scotia to accept an honorary degree at Acadia University the Minister of Finance referred to the economic survey being planned. He said, and I have no reason to doubt his word, that special consideration will be given to the economic aspects and problems of the Atlantic region. We hope this purpose will be carried out. It serves as an illustration of what I have been saying, that special attention should be paid to the regional aspect of the matter.
Then I have two other points in mind. I believe many will agree when I say there should be closer co-operation among various departments of government. This lack of cooperation has a particularly unfortunate effect on labour when one considers that in connection with such matters as immigration and labour, for example, there are so many overlapping duties and responsibilities. Yet we do not know of any co-ordination between these branches of government. I imagine that there is a considerable amount of co-operation; but surely the time has arrived when we must really get together. If this were done it would eliminate much of the trouble we now have in connection with the distribution of immigrants.
For instance, it was only a few days ago that the hon. member for Quebec West referred to the surplus labour force available at Seven Islands. I am not saying anyone is responsible for this; I am simply pointing out that if there had been a close liaison between the immigration branch and the Department of Labour this condition at Seven Islands might have been avoided. It would seem that this is another suggestion falling within the ambit of those special duties which, it seems to me, rest with the Department of Labour.
Then it would seem that there could be closer co-operation between the Department of Finance and the Department of Labour. I was interested reading the other day in a United States newspaper about a method used in the United States to eliminate labour surplus areas. I do not know whether it would be possible to implement such a plan in Canada but, briefly, in the United States it appears that groups interested in finance and labour are charged with the responsibility of getting together and making decisions as to whether certain areas are labour surplus areas. The labour surplus condition could develop from a local economic condition, such as the shutting down of an industry, or for some other reason. Under this scheme, when an area is declared labour surplus it is given official assistance by the federal

authority. In this way defence and other industries can locate where labour surplus is in evidence, and thus receive federal assistance.
I would like to apply that principle to the maritime provinces and, in particular, to the situation at Marysville. At that point there was a shut-down of industry, and a special problem developed. However, a very skilful labour surplus was available there. Why would it not have been possible for some other industry to come in and make use of that labour surplus? I suggest, further, that it might have been possible for the department to work out with the Department of Finance some scheme of special tax concessions, perhaps involving amortization over a period of 20 years and permitted as a deduction from the federal taxes imposed on an industry.
Had such an inducement been offered an industry may have been able to come in and locate. As the situation stands today the municipality must bear the responsibility. It must offer various tax concessions and assessment relief and, as we know, the municipalities cannot afford special assistance at that time. I do urge, therefore, that there be closer contact and co-operation among departments of government.
There is one further matter I would discuss with the minister, and that is the matter of local advisory committees. We have in Canada many complex problems in local areas. In that connection I think immediately of the national harbours board, which today is big business. With the approval of the department, local advisory committees are being set up in the different ports to advise the permanent officials as to local needs and plans. I understand that for some time there have been local advisory employment committees in various areas of Canada.
I suggest, however, that the responsibility for the organization and co-ordination of these local committees should not be left to the local unemployment insurance officer. The department should make definite plans for co-operation, and should advise how a group could function. I realize that there may be some interdepartmental advice and assistance in this connection, but I do feel there should be a greater measure of guidance and co-operation. For instance, recently the department published an interesting and useful booklet on the subject of older workers, setting out the problems of this group. I believe that publication was well received and probably was helpful in assisting those charged with the responsibility of looking after those workers.
In conclusion I should like to refer to an article to sort of tie in the suggestions I have

made. The article is entitled "This Changing Canada". It is taken from Canadian Business, published by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, and is dated May, 1955. It is mainly concerned with industrial growth and manufacturing, and was written by Richard L. Edsall. He is referring to employment in manufacturing and the increases that have taken place across Canada, and says:
Going 'way back, of course, you find a sharply different picture. In 1870, when the first Canadian census was taken. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick employed 18 per cent of the country's factory workers; by 1952 this figure was only about 4 per cent. Even more surprising, those maritime provinces had a greater number of manufacturing employees in 1870 than they had 69 years later, in 1939. In the same 69 years, manufacturing employment in Quebec rose to 330 per cent of the 1870 level, and in Ontario to 365 per cent. The 1870 figures are not completely comparable with later ones, but even so they show in startling relief both the relative and absolute decline of manufacturing in the maritimes.
Further on, Mr. Speaker, the author has this to say:
This points up, once again, the need to study regional as well as over-all national changes. It may be clear enough on a national scale, for instance, that the food and beverage industries have slipped in relative importance. But if you unthinkingly assume that this applies more or less equally to all areas including the maritimes and prairies, you will miss seeing the true impact that this industry's rate of growth can have locally.
I leave that with the minister and his department. I should just like to say that the economic picture in the maritimes is very good. We are quite optimistic about the future. But I do feel that some of our modes of life and regional considerations, particularly labour, must be given that extra help we need to put us back on a very good national footing.

I have no intention of holding up the passing of this item, but I wish to take a few minutes chiefly to correct the history of the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Before I spend a few moments on the history of the Leader of the Opposition, may I take a minute or two to congratulate him on his fine television performance last night. It was as expert a performance as I have seen, at least since I saw the Minister of Fisheries a week or so ago. If they both keep on improving they will soon be in the class of Anne Francis, who is also very photogenic.
The history of the Leader of the Opposition that I particularly want to refer to was not so much the particular point he made last night, but rather the remarkable statement he made the other day that the Conservative party in Canada was entirely responsible for bringing about confederation. That amazed me for
Supply-Labour two reasons; first because of where I sit in this house, and second as a former associate editor of the Toronto Globe, I am sure that particular statement would have been news indeed to the founder of that paper, the late Hon. George Brown. Therefore I want to suggest in all kindliness that I hope the next time we have a party in the railway committee room I shall have the privilege of pointing out to the Leader of the Opposition that sitting right in the middle of the fathers of confederation is Hon. George Brown, who certainly was not a member of the Conservative party. If I remember correctly, the reason the Conservative party for about 60 years used the title "Liberal Conservative party" was the contribution made by the Liberals as well as the Conservatives to the confederation of Canada.
I do not intend to go into the rather remarkable version of history given yesterday by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in regard to the Winnipeg strike. I happen to know a great deal about that strike, because I had partly written a novel about it. I think it was about the worst novel ever written in Canada. It was so bad I threw it away. In any event, I had to do a lot of studying of the Winnipeg strike to write it.
Without labouring the point, apart from the fine speech I mentioned in the house yesterday, made by the dean of the house the hon. member for Quebec South, if the hon. member will look at the speech made by the uncle of the present member for the Magdalen islands, the late Lucien Cannon, he will see that the version of history he gave yesterday was certainly not complete. There were voices raised in the house at that time about the mistakes that were made.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit an interjection?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I went only so far as to say that on June 6, 1919, there was no opposition offered by the Liberal party. That was the only point being discussed at that time.

I welcome that interjection. It is because I know the hon. gentleman opposite has such a high regard for accuracy that I did not think it was a good thing that a mistaken impression should go into the records of this house.

On a question of privilege, I should like to remind the hon. member that when he spoke of the late Hon. Lucien Cannon as being the member for the Magdalen islands, he never was.

Supply-Labour
No; you should listen more carefully.

I may tell the hon. member for Quebec West that I was referring to the uncle of the present member for the Magdalen islands.
There are two other points I wish to discuss for a minute or two, Mr. Chairman. The first is to give what support 1 can to the very eloquent plea made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, namely for a study of ways and means to help fit into the Canadian picture the people who have got beyond the age when they find it easy to get steady employment. That is something which should be close to the hearts and should be engaging the minds of all members in this house. The second point is to give very definitely qualified support, strictly qualified support, to the recommendation made not long ago by the hon. member for Spadina, with whom I almost always agree, on the question of a study of the guaranteed annual wage. I say I give it qualified support because one of the reasons I believe it should be very carefully studied is that I am by no means convinced that the guaranteed annual wage, as it has been advocated so far in Canada, would be on balance a good thing for all ordinary working people in Canada.
Perhaps it could become a good thing for certain industries. On another occasion some time ago the hon. member for Hamilton West referred to the stop and go system in the manufacture of railway cars. Perhaps through better planning and more systematic purchasing by the two railways we could have something more in the nature of steady employment, which in turn would help to give in effect a guaranteed annual wage. It does seem to me that in any industry where the workers and the management could get together and could show how, by stabilizing employment, they could cut costs and give consumers of Canada products at lower prices, then of course you could justify the guaranteed annual wage on that basis.
But, Mr. Chairman, I am frank to say that the great danger I see is the rather indiscriminate and unstudied advocacy of the guaranteed annual wage as a mere slogan. I would think any large employer of labour in Canada who was compelled to accept the principle of a guaranteed annual wage when he felt it was not in his own interests to do so, who was compelled to keep on his payroll all year round a certain number of workers whether or not they could be profitably employed, would feel inclined to cut back or drastically reduce the number of workers he -would retain on his payroll.

I am not stating that as my studied conclusion. I am simply stating it as a reason for urging upon the Minister of Labour that before too long a proper body be set up to study all the effects of the guaranteed annual wage. I for one do not believe we will ever get ahead in this country if this guaranteed annual wage is brought about as a result of the coercion of one side or the other in industry. I do not believe in the coercion of workers, and in the state of society in which we live I do not believe in the coercion of the people who provide employment. I think a guaranteed annual wage would be a great mistake unless it was shown to the employer as well as to the worker that it was to their mutual interest.

Mr. Chairman, obviously the discussion on the first item of the estimates of the Minister of Labour has opened up quite a wide field of debate. Naturally I am tempted to pursue the line which has just been followed by the hon. member for Vancouver South with reference to what he has termed as the guaranteed annual wage but which I think is being more aptly termed in some quarters as the guaranteed employment year. The danger he mentioned of a cut-back in productive activity is undoubtedly an important consideration in that connection. I was pleased to note that this was a subject for considerable study in the research carried on by the U.A.W. union. If the hon. member has not studied some of their proposals I commend them to his attention.
At the beginning of his remarks the hon. member for Vancouver South gave us another chapter in the history lesson we have had during the course of this debate. I do not intend to participate in that history lesson, but I am rather tempted to move for a few moments into the realm of philosophy which was being pursued last night by the hon. member for Prince Albert. Those hon. members who heard his remarks will recall that at the beginning of his speech the hon. member gave us quite a philosophical discourse upon the ramifications of the industrial revolution as it affected employment. He referred to some remarks that had been made earlier by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. The hon. member for Prince Albert had this to say in part, and I quote from page 3939 of Hansard of May 19 as follows:
While each generation fears that mechanization will reduce employment, each generation in succession has found that while mechanization has expanded to a degree beyond the belief of anyone of even 50 years ago, nonetheless employment has been extending by the extending field of other production.

The hon. member had prefaced that general statement by suggesting that he felt the hon. member for Cape Breton South had but repeated a rather old fear which has always been with men since the beginning of the industrial revolution, that as inventiveness makes possible a greater production it also brings about a continued and extensive unemployment.
I would venture to suggest that when it comes to making a philosophical analysis of our industrial society the hon. member for Cape Breton South penetrated just as far into those implications as did the hon. member for Prince Albert. The hon. member for Cape Breton South is quite aware that over the course of years new fields of productivity have been opened up. I think that problem was very much in his mind, and I should like to quote his words as recorded on page 3919 of Hansard, as follows:
Within the next few years we are going to find that automation will be putting more and more men on the street and we will be faced with the problem of retraining men for some other gainful occupation.
Earlier the hon. member had posed the question of whether man was going to be master of the machine or the machine master of man. It would appear to me that in that statement and in his reference to the need of retraining the men who are going to be replaced he was pointing out to this house that in the process of the industrial transformation which is proceeding, as he suggested at an ever-increasing pace, we must not lose sight of what that process has done and is doing to the human beings who are involved. That seemed to me more to the point in a discussion of the estimates of the Minister of Labour than to ramble into philosophical generalities indulged in by the hon. member for Prince Albert. Unless the Minister of Labour and every hon. member of this house are concerned with what is happening to the human beings involved, an expanding productivity does not mean a great deal.
I shall pursue this matter only to the point of using one illustration of how we cannot disregard the effect this changing technology has on the lives of human beings. An event took place in my own district within the last year or two. At various times there was a suggestion in the local press that the Department of National Defence had plans to build something like 100 houses to provide accommodation for the personnel of the air station. The fact that this was in contemplation was a matter of great interest to those concerned in the construction trades. As these
Supply-Labour
reports continued they anticipated, and I would say quite rightly, that when that construction project was undertaken they would have an opportunity for employment. As individuals they may have qualified for benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act, and as people with homes in that district they naturally made their plans according to the prospects. Rather than leave their homes and go to some distant part of the country they said, "We will stick it out; we have this prospect of a period of useful employment before us, and we are going to stay put."
Then a decision was made that these houses were not to be built directly under the auspices of the government, but rather that a plan setting up a limited dividend housing corporation would be the best way to deal with that situation. I am not suggesting at the moment that was not the best way of dealing with that particular situation, but the point I am trying to make is that once that step was taken the opportunity for employment in that area where this action had been anticipated suddenly vanished into thin air. It was announced that the houses were going to be erected as prefabs, and that the prefabs were going to come from another part of the country.
That is an example in a small way of the unnecessary uncertainty which individual workingmen have to face as the technology of production changes. Somehow or other it should have been possible for those men to have been forewarned that their prospective means of livelihood was going to be whisked out from underneath them because of another method of housing production. The fact that it may be a more efficient and economical method of housing production is small comfort to those tradesmen, who because of that situation have lost some work at wages that would have enabled them to live in comfort and decency. That is the kind of problem I, as a member of this house, have in the back of my mind.
I heard the hon. member for Cape Breton South suggesting the need for retraining, and I would add the words "and reorientation", of the working people of this country to meet these changing conditions. One of our responsibilities in this house is to apply our minds and our thoughts to how that can be done, and that is one of the responsibilities which we hope the Minister of Labour and his department will be increasingly willing to assume as time goes on.
This debate has gone on at some length, and I intend at this time to mention only one other point. I should like to add a few words in support of what was suggested

Supply-Labour
by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in respect to the need for consideration of a wider coverage, tied in with unemployment insurance, for unemployment resulting from illness. I suggest that increasingly the normal pattern for coverage against loss of income from sickness is becoming closely allied to the pattern which has been followed under our unemployment insurance plan. I know that in the area from which I come a very large number of workers are covered for that purpose by various local arrangements between employers and employees and various insurance companies. The pattern in its application is very close to that of the present unemployment insurance plan. Employer and employee each contributes half the cost of that plan; the premium is paid by a payroll deduction, and benefits payable are in many instances somewhat comparable to those which are made out of the unemployment insurance fund. So, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that it is becoming increasingly evident that a much more logical, efficient and economical arrangement would be to have that type of coverage closely allied with our present unemployment insurance arrangements on a national scale.
I have heard the Minister of Labour discuss and advocate the need for greater mobility of labour in this country. I suggest that one of the greatest disadvantages of the present type of plan which covers people for loss of income through sickness is that it tends to make labour more immobile, that a man is not able to move from one employer to another without losing the coverage for sickness that he may have enjoyed in his former employment. The only logical way such a plan can be developed is through some such agency as we have in our unemployment insurance commission.
I suggest that there is really no great reason why any serious objection to that development should come from the employing interests. I know on a good many occasions I have heard people in management, particularly in the office end of management, complaining about the time-consuming efforts in which they have to engage in order to make the multiplicity of payroll deductions involved. Here is a manner in which great economies, taken in total, could be effected. All deductions and all arrangements and correspondence involved could be combined and simplified to bring about a broader basis of coverage, both for unemployment through loss of a job and unemployment because of sickness. These two could be combined in one simple deduction plan that would cover workers not only in a particular firm at a particular time but 
also wherever they might be called upon to go in the course of finding useful work within our Canadian economy.

Mr. Chairman, as we all know, each month the dominion bureau of statistics and the Department of Labour issue a news release showing the unemployment for the previous month. In May, 1953, this release was made on the 20th day of the month. In May, 1954, the release was made on the 19th day of the month. Last month, April, the release was made on the 19th day of the month. Today is the 20th day of May, and there has been no sign-
Yesterday was a holiday.

-of the appearance of any news release showing unemployment in April. The material that goes into these news releases is available for several days before the news release is made. If you look at the news release, you will see the heading states that it is to be made available at ten a.m. on a certain date. The material is not just made available on that date, of course; it is known several days before, and there is no doubt that the Department of Labour is familiar with that figure today.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I believe we are entitled to ask why this release has not been made public. I think it is for the same reason that consideration of the estimates of this department was pushed forward ahead of the estimates of the Post Office Department, so the government could try to get the labour discussion out of the way before it became necessary to publish what are obviously going to be embarrassing figures regarding the unemployment situation.
Seeing that the government does not choose to make these important figures available at the time they should, when this debate is in progress, I think it is only fair that we should examine past figures and try to estimate what the figure is likely to be. If you examine the figures for the past three years you will notice there is a fairly consistent pattern of increases and decreases in unemployment, as employment ebbs and flows during the periods of relatively high and low employment in these years.
Let us take, for example, the first four months of the last two years and compare them. In 1954 unemployment in February increased over January by 7 per cent. This year unemployment in February increased over January by 8 per cent. In 1954 unemployment in March increased over February by 2 per cent. This year unemployment in March increased over February by 3 per

cent. So you will see there is a fairly consistent pattern month by month, and it holds good if you go back several years.
In 1954 unemployment in April decreased from the March figure by 3J per cent. In estimating what the figure may be for April of this year, I think it is fair to assume that as unemployment increased this year at a slightly greater rate for the two previous months, it would decrease at a slightly greater rate than last year for the month of April. Therefore, instead of assuming that unemployment would decrease from March at the same rate as last year, 3J per cent, I think it is fair to assume it would decrease by 4J per cent from March. Applying that figures to the March unemployment figure of 633,000, I arrive at an estimated unemployment figure for April of 605,000.
That is the situation, Mr. Chairman, which I believe the government are most anxious to hide. They are most anxious to hide it because they described the unemployment situation as merely seasonal and regional in referring to it in the speech from the throne. When the suggestion was made to the Minister of Labour that he might extend supplementary benefits beyond April 15 his reply was, "Well, after all, there will not be many unemployed at that time."
As I have pointed out, there are a great many unemployed as of this time, and there were a great many unemployed during the whole winter when the Prime Minister refused to deal with the matter. He brushed it aside as something of no consequence and finally, when he did come to deal with it because of the great pressure brought to bear on him by opposition members of parliament and the provincial premiers, he put forward to the provinces a proposition that can only be termed a cheap substitute for the proposition put forward in 1945 by this same government. It is a cheap substitute put forward by a government which in 1941 and 1945 accepted the principle of federal responsibility for unemployed employables.
The offer put forward by the Prime Minister at the dominion-provincial conference is very inadequate, because it places far too heavy a load on the provincial and municipal levels of government, which do not have the sources of taxation available to bear these very heavy costs.
I think the most important thing of all in the handling of the unemployment situation by the government to date is the fact that the government has refused to make any attempt to meet the need of providing more jobs in the country today. If the government refuses to face this need, then it is up to opposition members of parliament to make
Supply-Labour
suggestions in the hope that perhaps in a year or two, after the government is sure that no credit will accrue to the opposition for such suggestions, they might possibly be adopted.
Let us look at the possibilities in this country for increasing job opportunities. We live in a country that can produce enough food to support several times our present population. We have almost limitless sources of hydroelectric power, coal, oil, natural gas, and uranium from which we can produce atomic energy. We have also almost limitless supplies of timber, iron ore, copper, zinc, lead, nickel and practically every other mineral that is used in manufacturing industries today. Yet for some unknown reason we in this country seem perfectly satisfied to ship most of our mineral wealth out of the country in its raw state, and buy back much of it in the form of finished articles which have been processed in other countries, thereby giving employment to foreign workmen.
I think it is about time we asked ourselves why we do not process far more of our raw materials right here in Canada and provide jobs for Canadian workmen, instead of being content to go on month after month with unemployment figures in excess of 600,000 and not be willing to face the fact that something must be done about this critical situation. You cannot keep on passing it off, as the government seem determined to do, as something of no consequence, something which is merely, to use their own words, seasonal and regional.
In addition to the raw materials we have right here in Canada, and the almost limitless sources of power of one kind or another, we also have large supplies of capital; and we have proved we can attract it from outside. We also have the supply of brains necessary to make an important industrial expansion possible. Why do we not do something about it? I am going to make some suggestions to the government as to what they can do to get this thing moving.
First of all, Mr. Chairman, we must realize that in a free country we cannot simply issue a command and have industrial expansion start. The government must create an attractive economic atmosphere within the country or new industries will not be started and present industries will simply not expand. You cannot just command them to do it. Unless we do create an attractive economic atmosphere in the country we are going to continue to be primarily a producer of raw materials to be shipped out of the country to provide work in foreign factories for foreign workmen,

Supply-Labour
and then buy back many of these finished products in Canada. That, to me is the ultimate in stupidity.
What should we do to create this attractive economic atmosphere? I am going to make five suggestions to the government, and I think they are practical suggestions. First of all, to encourage new industries to start and present industries to expand, I say we must make it easier for new industries to show their first profit. We can do that if we will reduce taxation on the first profits an industry makes.
As a suggestion, I urge that on the first $20,000 of profit, before taxes, we reduce the rate of tax from the present 18 per cent to 15 per cent, and raise the ceiling from $20,000 to $25,000. I believe the fact that the present rate of tax jumps, from 18 per cent on up to $20,000, to 47 per cent on the next $1,000 of profit is a severe handicap to the expansion of small industry. I believe the government would induce a great many small industries to expand beyond their present limits by making the increase beyond the top of the lower bracket, at the present time $20,000, to up to say $50,000 at an even rate instead of making a sudden jump to 47 per cent.
It is obvious that if two men who are in business are making $20,000 today, who by taking some chance could expand, find that by doing so they will have to give the government half of the next $1,000 they earn, they will go on producing at the same rate and not expand. However, if there were a steady rate of increase in taxation from say $20,000 up to $50,000 it would encourage the expansion of small industries which might turn into big industries.
Second, I suggest we make it possible to sell more goods, both here and abroad, by lowering our costs as a result of the reduction of sales taxes by at least 25 per cent. The government argue that this cannot be done because there will be a loss of revenue. Any businessman knows, Mr. Chairman, that if his cost is so high that he is losing business it becomes advantageous to him to reduce his selling price to the point where people will buy considerably more of his goods. He knows that the greater volume of goods sold, multiplied by a smaller unit profit will, if it is properly worked out, give him larger total net returns than formerly. In the same way, if we reduce the cost of the goods we sell by reducing our sales and excise taxes materially, it will make it possible to sell more goods. The larger volume of goods sold, multiplied by a smaller unit tax, may, I believe, very easily equal or exceed the present total tax revenue.
[Mr. Hees.l
The third suggestion I make is that we should make a really worth-while reduction in income taxes. The last income tax reduction was simply a token reduction. It amounted to less than 25 cents per week for a married man with two children earning the average income for Canada. Such a reduction is not going to do very much by way of stimulating sales or plant expansion. It is not going to make people rush out and buy goods or expand their plant.
I suggest that a substantial reduction in income tax be made in the interests of making it possible for people to buy more goods. If people buy more goods, more goods will be produced; more people will be employed producing those goods, and the government will be collecting more tax revenue on more goods sold. The government will also receive more income taxes as a result of more people being employed, instead of paying those people unemployment insurance benefits or direct relief. It is simply a matter of dollars and cents arithmetic in which this government seems unwilling to indulge.
The fourth suggestion I make is that we should reduce the risk involved in starting new enterprises by doubling the rate of depreciation on plant and equipment. If a man who is thinking of going into a new enterprise, which he believes is perhaps risky, knows that his money is only going to be tied up for half the length of time it would otherwise be, he will be more likely to take the chance. We have to make it attractive for people to put money into new enterprises. We cannot force people to invest money and start new enterprises. Unless people are willing to invest money, new enterprises simply will not get started.
The fifth suggestion I make is that we make it easier to sell our goods to other countries, and to attract tourists to Canada, by stabilizing our dollar with the United States dollar.
As I have said, the government claims that taxes cannot be reduced because that would result in a loss of revenue. I say the only way we are going to solve this unemployment problem, the only way we are going to make it possible for Canadians who want to work to have productive jobs, is to create economic conditions in this country which will make it attractive for people to start new enterprises, and for people who are in small enterprises to expand. Unless people want to do these things they will not be done and our country will remain primarily a producer of raw materials which will be shipped out of the country to provide employment for people elsewhere.
When speaking last September the Prime Minister said that if the government was not

smart enough to arrange its affairs so everybody could have a job, then it was incompetent. Having made some suggestions here today in a very serious frame of mind, to which I hope the government will give serious consideration, I believe that by following these suggestions the government could cure the incompetence which the Prime Minister, on their behalf, has admitted exists today.

I should like to ask the hon. member a question. He has suggested reducing income taxes substantially, and reducing sales taxes. Where would he get some revenue to enable the government to carry on its business?

I have tried, Mr. Chairman, to explain to the hon. member for Fort William and other members in the house how this would be accomplished, but I shall do it again. If you are making a limited volume of sales because your costs are high-this is the sort of thing any businessman has to calculate every day of the year-then you must reduce your costs and increase your sales. I am suggesting that by lowering the sales tax materially we would lower the cost of the goods we have to sell, thus making them more competitive with the foreign goods that are entering the country today. If we can sell more goods, then we will be able to tax more goods and the greater volume of goods sold multiplied by the smaller unit tax will possibly equal or exceed the present total tax revenue. If you make it possible to sell more goods you have more people employed. Instead of drawing unemployment insurance or direct relief, these people will be earning incomes on which they will be paying income tax, and that would be added revenue to the government.
I suggest that by adopting the ideas I have put forward you will create conditions in the country which will attract capital investment in new enterprises and enable present enterprises to expand, and create a condition in the country which will mean the employment of many more people and the production of a great deal more goods. By so doing we will increase the sources which produce taxes, increase the number of income tax payers and the volume of goods sold, and I believe by careful operation we can in the long run considerably increase our tax take. Surely this is well worth trying.
But it is not so easy.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer to a matter which perhaps could be discussed more properly under item 178. However, I shall bring it forward now so the minister may give it
Supply-Labour
consideration during the dinner hour and be in a position to state the government's position.
There is being circulated within the ranks of the government a document which I find stupid and utterly obnoxious, and which conceivably could be used in a wicked way. To my way of thinking it is a document which is quite illegal, because we have passed legislation banning this sort of nonsense. I hold the minister responsible because there is no one else I can hold responsible. In saying that I am not saying I believe for one minute that he has connived at what is going on or, indeed, that he condones it. However, he is responsible to the house for what I consider to be a violation of the law.
Two years ago all parties joined in hailing the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. The minister will remember the acclaim it received and the manner in which is was passed through the house because it filled a need, in the view of many of us. We think, too, that it has proven its usefulness.
I, for one, have never seen any sense in these application forms for employment in which questions are asked concerning the nationality and racial origin of applicants. I have always assumed that a person would be given a job because of his or her inherent ability, and not for any other reason. Now we find that in this act it says in section 4(5):
No person shall use or circulate any form of application for employment or publish any advertisement in connection with employment or prospective employment or make any written or oral inquiry in connection with employment that expresses either directly or indirectly any limitation, specification or preference as to race, national origin, colour or religion unless the limitation, specification or preference is based upon a bona fide occupational qualification.
That is the law of the land. Yet I have in my hand this document which, I assume, is circulated throughout all departments of government. I make that assumption because no one particular department is named. This purports to be a personal history form. What are the questions asked? They are those which parliament agreed should be banned from such forms.
For instance, the applicant is asked to give his nationality. Yet in the subsection I read that is forbidden. The applicant is here asked to give his racial origin; again the subsection forbids it. Surely the government is not going to continue to violate the statute.
Then the document becomes even more stupid, because on the next page it asks for the names of immediate relatives, wife, husband, sons or daughters over 16. It asks for the names of the father, mother, brothers and sisters, including blood relatives and deceased parents. Then the government

Supply-Labour
wishes to know the country of birth of a deceased parent. The government wishes to know the country of birth of step-relatives and blood relatives. What conceivable use can it make of such information? And if it cannot make use of that information, why ask such stupid questions? If it is going to use the information, then why is it to be used?
Aiter all, what has my father's birthplace to do with my capacity to hold down a job? What has my mother's birthplace to do with my ability to do a job? What has the birthplace of my in-laws to do with my loyalty to Canada? Yet these questions are asked here. And not only are they asked in respect of the applicant, but also his wife-parents, wife or husband, date and country of birth.
I maintain that these questions are utterly unforgivable, in view of the legislation passed by the house and also in view of the protestations made by various members of the government. I bring the matter up because I would like the minister to find out during the dinner hour just what the government's policy is, whether it is going to pay any attention to the statements which were made in parliament two years ago, or whether it is going to continue issuing what I described earlier, and I suggest most correctly, as a stupid and obnoxious document.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry the hon. member for Prince Albert is not in his seat, because at the outset of my remarks I want to comment on some expressions he used the other day. I wish I could share his optimism when he suggests that what we are witnessing in our industrial society is merely a repetition of what has happened before, and that the massive displacement of human labour that we see immediately ahead of us carries no more dangerous implications for our society than did the more primitive developments of past years.
I would point out, too, that even during those periods when much slower and much less fundamental changes were taking place, the consequences of which the hon. member for Prince Albert dismisses so cavalierly, there were many thousands of people whose lives were ruined, many thousands of people who faced a complete blank wall so far as earning their livelihood was concerned. It was not a light matter with them.
But today we are facing something much more fundamental and much more important than that. I heard the other day about a plant in Ontario in connection with which it was revealed that a couple of years ago, after all taxes and costs were paid, it had more funds in net profits than were paid out in wages and salaries. This was not because
[Mr. Stewart (Winnipeg North).)
the wages and salaries were low because, in fact, they were not; they were among the highest in industry. It was because the human element of production in that particular industry has become such an unimportant factor.
Out in my own constituency we have a similar development. I want to deal with this in detail, because I think it illustrates the real nature of the problem the government and the people of Canada face today. We have in my constituency one of the largest wood pulp factories on the Pacific coast. A few years ago it was doubled in size. Just before that doubling process took place there was a merger between two very large forest products corporations. At the time the merger took place the company to which I am referring sent a prospectus to all its employees, respecting the two merged companies, explaining their plans for the future. They were very frank about their plans and their financial position, and told their employees they were going to build an addition to the plant at a cost of $17 million. All of this was to be paid out of surplus earnings of the previous few years. They said that when this addition, costing $17 million, was completed, there would be work for 100 more employees.
That, I suggest, gives some idea of the sort of problem we are facing today. When we break this down we find that it represents an investment of $170,000 per man employed. And when we realize that the cost of that investment, and the returns, must be paid by the labour of those employed in the plant, we find this rather startling picture.
The average wage in that industry was at that time $3,600 a year. Each of the 100 workers would have to produce $3,600 worth of wealth to pay his wages, to start with. He would then have to make enough to pay the depreciation on a new plant. If you put that at the very modest figure of 5 per cent for buildings and equipment-and I am quite sure it would be very much more than that- then he would have to produce, in addition to the $3,600 for wages, $8,500 worth of wealth to pay for the depreciation charges. Then presumably there would be some return on the investment, and if you put that at another modest 5 per cent we would have another $8,500. So each of these 100 new workers must produce $20,600 worth of wealth during the year, otherwise that plant cannot function.
I am mentioning this not with any suggestion at all that the workers in that industry are hard done by, or are being exploited or robbed; they are not. They are well paid,

and the jobs are not very arduous. But I want to point out the discrepancy between the volume of wealth produced and the volume distributed in wages for its production, which creates for us the most appalling problems for the future.
The developments we have had in the past and the developments we have today differ not merely in degree but actually in kind. I hold in my hand a book published five years ago by Dr. Norbert Wiener, of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, a man who had a very large part to play in the development of the modern computing "machines of judgment", as they are now called. In this book he has some very interesting comments to make on the effect on society of the sort of machines that are now being produced. He points out that hitherto our technological developments had been confined to replacing human muscle power, or animal muscle power, but now we are producing machines that take over many of the functions of judgment that have hitherto been exercised by human beings.
He has this to say with regard to the completely automatic production unit that he sees for the future, and he suggests that the period that will elapse between the time this book was written five years ago and the time when such completely automatic units of production will become a commonplace in American industry will be from 10 to 15 years, provided we do not get involved in a war, and provided that we survive a war. He points out that if we got engaged in a war there is no doubt whatever that we would have almost a complete automation of industry within five years, from sheer necessity. He puts the figure at about 10 to 15 years. Five of those years have now gone and he has this to say about the effects:
I have spoken of the actuality and the imminence of this new possibility. What can we expect of its economic and social consequences? In the first place, we can expect an abrupt and final cessation of the demand for the type of factory labour performing purely repetitive tasks. In the long run, the deadly uninteresting nature of the repetitive task may make this a good thing and the source of leisure necessary for man's full cultural development. It may also produce cultural results as trivial and wasteful as the greater part of those so far obtained from the radio and the movies.
Then he has this to say:
Let us remember that the automatic machine, whatever we think of any feelings it may have or may not have, is the precise economic equivalent of slave labour. Any labour which competes with slave labour must accept the economic conditions of slave labour. It is perfectly clear that this will produce an unemployment situation, in comparison with which the present recession and even the depression of the thirties will seem a pleasant joke. This depression will ruin many
Supply-Labour
industries-possibly even the industries which have taken advantage of the new potentialities. However, there is nothing in the industrial tradition which forbids an industrialist to make e sure and quick profit, and to get out before the crash touches him personally.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this is the real nature of the problem we are facing; that it is not merely a temporary displacement of labour and its reabsorption in some other part of our economy. I suggest we are facing something much more fundamental, because hitherto all our assumptions of the way in which we should operate society have been based on this, that every man has to some degree or other something of value to exchange for a livelihood. Maybe he has not very much, and he gets a very poor livelihood.
Today we can see the virtual displacement of the man who has nothing but his untrained muscular power. He is the man who lands on our relief rolls at the first touch of a recession. We are beginning to see the displacement of men with semi-skilled abilities, and now we see right in front of us the imminent certainty of the displacement of men with skilled abilities for whom there is now no opening in our industries in the production of goods and services.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, that our Department of Labour should be making a very intensive study of the possible effects of the distribution of goods and services, the distribution of wealth in this country, by the development of these new types of "machines of government", as a French scientist describes them, because it is something entirely new. It is not merely an extension of the old machines we have seen in the past, and it is literally going to bring us to the point where we will have goods produced and no one in receipt of income to consume them.
I was interested the other day to hear the hon. member for Cartier deal with this problem. He obviously realizes as well as anyone that we are faced with the danger of being strangled in the enormous volume of our own production, and our danger lies in the fact that we cannot get it distributed and consumed. His solution was that we should bring more immigrants into the country to consume the goods. That sounds like a reasonable proposition, but unfortunately there is a bit of a catch in it. There was a time when it might have been considered, shall we say, an economic nuisance that people who produced had also to consume; that we had to let the worker have a certain amount or he would die on us and would not be able to produce anything more. Today the picture is completely transformed, and it is a considerable economic nuisance to society that the

Supply-Labour
person who consumes has also to produce. The new immigrant the hon. member for Cartier wants to bring in to absorb the surplus products will, unfortunately, be obliged, by the very conditions under which we operate our society, to himself produce, and add further to the flood of goods.
No, Mr. Chairman, we are not going to find a solution to this problem by the old assumptions. We are not going to find it by the reduction of taxation, by the reduction of income tax and sales tax and exemptions from taxation to encourage new investment. We are up against a fundamental change in our society even more profound than that which began to take place 150 years ago.
I would hope to see the government provide for the Minister of Labour a considerable sum of money to enable him to do necessary research into this problem before we are flooded with a mass of unemployed for whom we have no hope and whose conditions we are unequipped to help. I see the minister smiling agreement with that. I would suggest, however, that when he undertakes this inquiry and this investigation he should not be deterred by the fact that it is going to reveal to him that the old assumptions of free enterprise have gone by the board forever.
I was just smiling at the many demands of yesterday and today that I have the Department of Labour conduct studies on so many matters.

Most of them will be directed to those gloom gatherers over here to my left, because some things have been said in this house in the last couple of days that display such an astonishing lack of confidence in this country of ours and this system of ours that it is about time somebody rose in his place and pointed out some of the weaknesses and fallacies in their arguments. I wonder if there has ever been a more unrealistic statement made in a labour debate. Such a statement simply flies in the face of every experience we have had in

Down through history we find that the more mechanization there has been, the greater production and the more jobs there were for people. I dare say that if the hon. member for Nanaimo had been in the house in those days he would have voiced the same opinion.
Of course their hindsight is much better than was their foresight. They are ready to stand up here and say that the things which have happened in the past have no relationship to those which are going to

I suppose when the telephone first came in they might not have objected because new jobs were being created, but when they came along and proposed to use the dial telephone instead of the manual telephone they would consider that an absolute disaster.
I can just imagine them making speeches about how the telephone operators would be thrown out of work with the use of the dial telephone. We all know what has happened. Telephone service became so reasonable, the use of telephones increased to such an extent that we now find that more girls are coming out of the long distance exchange in Montreal alone than were employed servicing the manual installation throughout the city.

They have a tremendous number more, and that is what I am telling you. Then, if these hon. members had been around thousands of years ago when someone first got the idea of the wheel I know they would have said that that was an absolutely dangerous thing because it would mean, in the case of the thousands who had been put to work building the pyramids, that only five people would be needed to pull up a piece of stone instead of 500. today can see that. Because of weaknesses, stupidity and shortsightedness on the part of the government that sits over there today, we have more unemployment than we should have. We have more problems than we should have, but it is no indication that we are going to solve them by taking people who know even less than the present government, if that is possible, and carrying out their ideas.
I wish to say, Mr. Chairman, that industry and business of this country have their biggest stake in keeping people at work and keeping their purchasing power up. Having said that, I wish to say that I have not the slightest fundamental worry about the advent of automation, the increased use of machinery and the other problems which face us. I have confidence in the businessmen of this country to find the solution to these problems.
