I
know that these changes, which are bound to come and which we see coming, are not going to come overnight. That is the basis of all these arguments we have heard advanced in the last day and a half. They seem to think that these changes are going to come overnight. They are not going to come overnight; they are going to come gradually; and the opportunity will be given to our workers and to our people to retrain themselves, to relocate themselves and to prepare themselves for a greater economy and a higher standard of living than anything we have ever known.
Let my last sentence be that the most serious obstacle which stands in the way of our progress to bigger and better things in this country today is the crackpot theories and the peculiar ideas-
Of the Conservative party.

-which are being advanced by these two heterogeneous collections of individuals on my left and the poorly administered government of this country, for which the gentlemen who sit opposite me must take the blame.

I had not intended to take up the time of the house this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, but after sitting here for several days listening to the various arguments on the minister's estimates, I think I should add my voice.
Some hon. members have said to me, "You are a labour man; are you not going to speak on this question?" I have answered that I do not think it is necessary on every occasion, and I cannot at this time be asking for too

much for labour after hearing the very soulful and heartrending stories of how the farmer has been faring in the last year or two. It is certainly time that we did take a look at the variation in farm income and those in industry. Farm income is steadily declining, and for that reason, as I have said, I feel that labour is faring not too badly. I note that we have had speaking this afternoon the hon. member for Broadview, an ex-brigade major and a manufacturer, certainly not in the labouring class; we have had the hon. Leader of the Opposition, P.C., Q.C., and the former president of the chamber of commerce; and we have also had speaking on this question the hon. member for Hamilton West, a P.A.
So now we come to the member for Kootenay East with "M.M." after his name, which simply stands for master mucker. I have had some connection with labour and have had calluses on my hands many times. I watched the hon. member for Broadview this afternoon using his hands to try to chop down the taxes on profits and income, and I could see the calluses plainly on the palms of his hands even at this distance. I have gone through the mill as a mucker, even up to the position of miner. "M.M." also stands for master of mineralogy. I can tell the members of the house that I do not share the anxiety of the hon. member for Nanaimo that automation or mechanization is going to do anything to injure the miners, the lumber workers or the farm workers. I did some mining and I can say with conviction that mining is really hard work.
You never quite recovered from it.

Quite obviously there is still a stoop to my back. The hon. member says I have not recovered from my efforts. That may be quite true. In the last 15 years I have seen very great changes in mining methods, and I think I can say, without being accused of bragging, that I have assisted in some ways in bringing about these improvements in methods. I can recall that not so long ago it took a crew of four miners four full shifts to drill a round in what we call chert, a very hard rock, and sometimes as high as eight shifts. The cost for labour ran as high as $50 a foot. The cost for powder and so on was of course very small, but in terms of actual labour effort and the return the cost ran into hundreds of dollars compared with the situation today. With the improvements in machines and the type of steel used, two miners today can drill the same round in four hours.
Supply-Labour
I had not intended speaking on this matter today but it so happens that only a day or two ago representatives from the miners' union were down here, and I asked them if they had any figures for last year as to the earnings of miners in the Sullivan mine. I recall that 15 years ago miners, working in the manner I have indicated and taking up to four days to drill a round, were earning about $8 a day. Mechanization has improved to the point where they can drill a round in four hours, and the figures given to me show that miners doing that particular type of work averaged up to $28 a day for the year.
That is an instance of mechanization not only making the work much easier but resulting in a great bonanza to the miners so far as remuneration for their work is concerned. To say that automation or mechanization is going to have a far-reaching ill effect is, in my opinion, simply nonsense. True, there are going to be some dislocations, but think of the people in the underdeveloped countries, such as in many parts of India, where there is no mechanization. There are beggars on the streets of the cities whose only way of making a living is to beg for 24 hours a day. The people in the rice fields sowing rice by hand are not unemployed, but I venture to say their circumstances are very much less favourable than those of any person in Canada. It is not that I do not have sympathy for those who are unemployed, but I think it is a very narrow view to take to fight mechanization and automation as the people in the textile industry did years ago in Great Britain.

May I ask the
hon. member a question? I just want to get this clear. Did he have the idea I was opposing automation and this development?

speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 374, to incorporate Petroleum Transmission Company.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member give the house an explanation of the bill?

The bill we are asked to approve is for the incorporation of Petroleum Transmission Company. This company is associated with Pacific Petroleum Limited, one of the pioneers if not the pioneer in oil and gas exploration in Alberta and Northern British Columbia. This company operated originally in the Turner valley field and later in the Leduc field and still later in the Red-water and other fields in Alberta. It now has substantial production of oil in Alberta from the Leduc and Redwater fields. Since 1949, the company has been particularly active in the exploration and development of oil and natural gas reserves in northern British Columbia and the adjoining areas of northwestern Alberta, particularly in that block known as the Peace river block which, as we know, comprises an area of northern Alberta and northern British Columbia lying astride the interprovincial boundary.
I have seen the operations of this company near Pouce Coupe, which as we know is very close to Dawson Creek, and also at Fort St. John, which is approximately 75 miles north of Dawson Creek on the Alaska highway. It would appear that the explorations of this company tend to move generally in a northwesterly direction towards the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. At the present time the company and its associates control

approximately four million acres of proven lands for potential oil and gas development.
It is the purpose of this Petroleum Transmission Company to build what might be called a grid or collection system to collect their products from these wells which are now operating and bring the products down for delivery to the main transmission lines such as Trans-Canada or Westcoast. It is because of the success and development of northern British Columbia that it has been possible to promise the supply of natural gas to Vancouver and parts of the northwestern United States. I might say, too, that much of the gas is wet gas and the liquid by-products such as propane and butane must be collected at a central point and delivered to a transmission system.
At the moment there is no intention of building a straight transmission line but just a collection grid system. With the future development it may be necessary, and they are asking authority, to build a transmission line themselves. I believe that is about all I need to say at the moment, Mr. Speaker, as I understand this bill will go to one of the standing committees where more details can be given.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. J. Mcllraiih (Ottawa West) moved
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 375, to incorporate Yukon Pipelines Limited.
Would the sponsor explain this bill?

It will be noted from the bill, Mr. Speaker, that the persons seeking incorporation are in the main officers of the White Pass and Yukon railway which was built at the time of the Klondike gold rush and extends from Skagway to Whitehorse, a distance of approximately 110 miles. In the year 1942 the United States army authorities built a pipe line along the railway right of way. After the end of the war the United States army continued to operate that pipe line to supply fuel oil from Skagway through Whitehorse and through a continuation of that line to their own forces in Alaska. In addition, they permitted the take-off of fuel oil at Whitehorse for Canadian needs.
Recently the United States authorities have built a pipe line from Haines, Alaska, to supply their own forces in Alaska. This new pipe line does not go through Whitehorse or the Yukon area. The agreement under which oil is taken off the line which comes over the railway route can be terminated on 30

days' notice. It is expected that when the new United States army line is brought into use, this one will be discontinued. The significance of that is that the people in the Whitehorse area and the Yukon area will be without any convenient supply of fuel oil. The incorporators are seeking authority to have a corporate capacity to negotiate to take over that pipe line if and when it is abandoned.
This bill is in the same form as other pipe line bills, but it is different in this way, that what is sought to be transported by this company is fuel oil in a refined state for use by consumers as opposed to the usual crude oil problem we have in connection with these pipe line bills. The bill itself also contains a geographical limitation to the British Columbia-Yukon area in Canada, but does contain a provision for the building of a pipe line outside of Canada. The reason for that, of course, is that the line does go through some 20 miles of Alaska. There is in the bill also a technical provision to which perhaps I should refer, and that is the power to build a line outside of Canada for the transmission of gas. This power is not limited. It would be the intention of the incorporators when the bill is in the committee stage to submit a limitation similar to the one put forward in another pipe line bill a few days ago, limiting to Canada the right to construct a pipe line for the transmission of gas.

It is my understanding, Mr. Speaker, that this proposed legislation is to provide a corporate vehicle for the operation as a common carrier of the existing pipe line between Skagway, Alaska, and Whitehorse, Yukon Territory. This pipe line is now owned and operated by the United States army, and is shortly to be de-activated and declared surplus. No doubt it will be disposed of through the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation.
The applicants for incorporation, as the hon. member has just said, are officers of the White Pass and Yukon Corporation Limited, who have had much experience in the operation of these facilities. I might mention also that the cheapest method of moving oil and gasoline into the Yukon Territory and surrounding area of northern British Columbia at the moment is by ocean tanker up the west coast to Skagway, Alaska, and thence by the existing four-inch pipe line through the mountains a distance of about 110 miles to Whitehorse. If this legislation is enacted it will provide for the continued operation of the existing four-inch pipe line between Skagway, Alaska, and Whitehorse, used for the transportation of
Private Bills
fuel and diesel oil, and for the eventual construction and operation of a new pipe line between the same points for the transportation of gasoline and petroleum products.
The opening up of the pipe line as a common carrier will make it possible for any other oil company that so desires to move its products up the coast and into Whitehorse on a competitive basis. The existing pipe line between Skagway and Whitehorse runs along the White Pass and Yukon railway right of way through precipitous and difficult mountain territory, winding its way to a height of over 3,000 feet in a matter of only 18 miles, crossing mountain bridges, through tunnels and under the protection of numerous snow sheds along the railway right of way.
The White Pass and Yukon road has been intimately associated with the operation of this line from its inception. The employees of the White Pass road are fully familiar with pumping and the other operating facilities of the system and are of course completely equipped to take over its operation.
When the United States army ceases to operate the line it appears natural therefore that the White Pass and Yukon route should function in its place, in view of the fact that the installations are chiefly on the railway right of way. I am, therefore, pleased to support this bill for the reasons given.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

Could we have an explanation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the situation with respect to this bill is somewhat similar to the one with which we have just dealt. The applicant, Trans-Prairie Pipelines, Ltd., was incorporated under the Companies Act of the province of Manitoba by letters patent dated August 5, 1954, for the purpose of acquiring, constructing, owning and operating oil pipe lines and gathering systems.
The applicant in particular was incorporated to acquire and operate a short pipe line and a gathering system connecting the Daly oil field near Virden in Manitoba to Cromer, a pumping station on the interprovincial pipe line, and also to construct an extension from the Daly field to the Virden Roselea and the North Virden Roselea oil fields. The extension to these latter fields was completed and put into operation late in 1954.
Portions of the present pipe line serving the Daly field were laid approximately eight miles from the Manitoba-Saskatchewan boundary.
The purpose of the present application is to secure authorization in the applicant company to extend its activities across the Manitoba-Saskatchewan boundary into southeastern Saskatchewan, as the progress of oil development in the area makes feasible the construction of pipe lines.
The applicant is particularly considering the possibility of constructing an oil pipe line to serve the Alida and Frobisher oil fields in southeastern Saskatchewan, and a possible extension from such an oil pipe line back into the province of Manitoba to serve the Tilson and Pearson oil fields in southwestern Manitoba.
As was mentioned in the discussion on the previous bill, under the Pipe Lines Act, the

applicant cannot construct or operate pipe lines crossing provincial boundaries without the authority of an act such as is asked in this instance.
I might add that the bill has been before the Senate and dealt with by the Senate committee which deals with these matters. It now comes to this house in its present form and, of course, will be submitted to a committee here, for further consideration.

Mr. Speaker, unfortunately this bill is not similar to the others which were read a second time this afternoon. If hon. members will refer to the three preceding bills, namely to incorporate Petroleum Transmission Company, to incorporate Yukon Pipelines Limited and to incorporate S & M Pipeline Limited, they will find that those bills are in the nature of charters incorporating companies.
They have extensive provisions. For example, they name the applicants for the charter; they provide for the first directors; they also regulate everything having to do with the capital stock. Then they go on to outline in detail the powers of the company which is to be incorporated by the bill, and deal with the question of loans to shareholders or directors and with the application of certain provisions of the dominion Companies Act. They also deal with the redemption or purchase for cancellation of paid up capital, and finally they deal with the paying of commission on subscription for shares, bonds, debentures and so on. In other words, they constitute the charter of the company.
On the other hand, the bill which we are now considering does not do that at all. It merely authorizes the company which has been set up under the Manitoba companies act to go into the pipe line business. If hon. members will refer to the bill they will find that there are none of these provisions that are contained in the other charters. This bill simply says that this Manitoba company has the power to construct pipe lines for both oil and gas. Nothing whatever is said about the people who are behind the bill. There are no restrictions on the capital structure of the company; there is nothing said about its powers. We have no idea what the powers of this company are. That will be contained in the papers filed in the office of the registrar of companies in Manitoba.
Nothing is said in the bill itself about where the pipe lines are to be built. Hon. members will notice that the other charters specifically set out that the pipe lines are to be built in certain parts of the country. For example, I take the S & M Pipeline Limited charter.
Private Bills
It says that the pipe lines are to be built in the Northwest Territories and in the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and outside Canada; but in the bill we are now considering absolutely no mention is made of where the pipe lines are to go. There is nothing to show that the company will be subject to the provisions of the dominion Companies Act, to which the other companies which have been given charters must submit, and there are none of the other restrictions which are contained in these other charters.
I do not see why one group should be able to come to this house and get a bill of this kind authorizing them to do everything that the other companies can do, which have come in and told their whole story and asked for charters of which we have the details. That appears to me to be discrimination, and also it opens the door wide to companies incorporated under a provincial companies act of any province of Canada. If TransPrairie Pipelines, Limited, can get authority in the terms set out in this bill, then 50, 100 or 1,000 provincially incorporated companies can do the same thing.
It opens the door wide, and in my opinion breaks down the whole basis set up by the Pipe Lines Act for the chartering of companies to go into the pipe line business. This is very big business, and very important, and the companies are given very extensive rights under the Pipe Lines Act. They have power to take lands, and all that sort of thing. They are given practically as wide powers as the railways. I submit that the intention of parliament, when it passed the Pipe Lines Act, was that in each case the people who wanted to go into the pipe lines business must come to parliament and get a charter. There has been only one case in which that was not done, and I intend to refer to it in a moment or two.
The Pipe Lines Act is chapter 211 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952. We find there that "company" is described as meaning:
A person having authority under a special act to construct or operate pipe lines for the transportation of oil or gas.
A "special act" is described as meaning:
An act of the parliament of Canada that authorizes a person named in the act to construct or operate pipe lines for the transportation of gas or oil or that is enacted with special reference to such pipe lines.
I suppose that technically the Trans-Prairie Pipelines, Limited, would be considered as a person and therefore technically this bill would come under that definition of a special act; technically getting an act through such as we are debating this afternoon might be

Private Bills
sufficient; but I do suggest that it would be against the whole spirit and intent of the Pipe Lines Act.
When we were discussing the amendment to the Pipe Lines Act in 1953 we were questioning the then minister of transport. I now quote from page 621 of Hansard of December 4, 1953, where Mr. Chevrier had this to say:
As I understand this amendment, it is still necessary for extra-provincial or interprovincial pipe lines to seek authority from this parliament by way of a special charter in order to apply to the board of transport commissioners for its location.
This shows clearly what the minister had in mind at that time. Mind you, there is no objection to a provincial company building a pipe line within the borders of that province. If Manitoba wants to incorporate a company to build a pipe line in Manitoba, then the Pipe Lines Act of the dominion does not apply. But that is not the case here. Presumably this company has already built lines in Manitoba and now intends to cross a border-I think the hon. member said the Saskatchewan-Manitoba border. Well, they may just as well want to cross an international border so far as the Pipe Lines Act is concerned. They should come to parliament and get a full charter in the same way that the other applicants have done over the last six years. It is six years now that applicants for charters have been coming here and complying with what I suggest is the real meaning of the act.
It is true that in 1954, a little over a year ago, the Niagara Gas Transmission Limited came here with a bill of the kind we are considering today, and I presume it is because that was done that Trans-Prairie Pipelines, Limited, are asking today for the same treatment. But the conditions were entirely different when Niagara Gas Transmission Limited came to parliament. They had been incorporated under the Ontario companies act. This company was a subsidiary of the Consumers Gas Company of Toronto and the Tennessee Gas Transmission Company of the United States. The parent companies had entered into a contract under which United States gas was to be imported into the greater Toronto area and part of the transmission of that gas was to be done by Niagara Gas Transmission Company. They were to pick up the gas in the middle of the Niagara river and bring it into the city of Toronto.
There was a great deal of discussion in the house. Hon. members will remember that the whole question of our gas policy was involved. It was felt that if Niagara Gas Transmission Limited went ahead as originally planned the result would be to prevent the construction of a trans-Canada pipe line

by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. In the final analysis an agreement was reached under which Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited built a pipe line in Canada from the middle of the Niagara river into the greater Toronto area.
There were all these special considerations behind the application for permission to Niagara Gas Transmission Limited to go into the pipe line business, but the fact that the charter was granted at that time should not establish a precedent for ordinary gas line charters. I do suggest that if this present policy is to be adopted, that is if this bill is passed by the house; if we allow these provincial companies to go into the interprovincial or international oil or gas transmission business merely by coming here and getting a bill through which permits them to go into business subject to the provisions of the Pipe Lines Act; if we are to be satisfied with a private bill of that kind, then we are opening the door wide to leaving parliament with practically no control over what such companies may do. We would be granting them the extremely wide powers contained in the Pipe Lines Act and in addition would be discriminating in a most unfair manner against Canadians who have followed the spirit and letter of the Pipe Lines Act by coming into this house with a bill which constituted a proper charter.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the sponsor of this bill is not present in the house and that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) has made an excellent argument as to why the bill should not be proceeded with in this form, I wonder if the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Weir) would recommend that the bill stand until another time. I do not think we should waste too much time debating it when the sponsor is not here. In my opinion a good case has not been made out for giving such wide powers to Trans-Prairie Pipelines, Limited, to approve the incorporation by letters patent without any more information than we have. We required the Westspur Pipe Line Company to tell us who are responsible and also something about the capital and their general plans. I wonder if the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa would indicate at this stage whether he would recommend that the bill stand until the hon. member who is sponsoring it is here to give further explanation.
Agreed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 379, to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the first comment I wish to make in moving the second reading of this bill is that I do so because of an interest in the principle raised by this bill. It would be useless for me to deny, even if I wanted to, that recent events have played some part in my bringing this legislation before the House of Commons at the present time. Nevertheless, my interest is not in any particular personality that might be involved but rather in a principle which has concerned this parliament and other parliaments for a great many years. That principle is set out in the question; should a cabinet minister at the same time be a director of a private company?
My interest in this question did not begin only two or three weeks ago. As a matter of fact when I first came to parliament in 1942 I was concerned to discover that it was not an absolute rule that a minister give up his directorships when he joins the cabinet. Accordingly, in an effort to draw attention
50433-251J
Senate and House of Commons Act to this fact and thereby to suggest, at least indirectly, that such a rule should be laid down, I have placed questions on the order paper of the House of Commons on at least three occasions. The first time I put those questions on the order paper, they were answered by sessional paper No. 296-A which was tabled in the House of Commons on June 5, 1943. That shows an interest of mine dating back some 12 years. The second time was a few years later when a sessional paper was tabled in response to certain similar questions of mine; this one was sessional paper No. 160-D, which was tabled on February 11, 1948. More recently I placed another set of questions on the order paper which was answered by sessional paper No. 173-A, tabled on April 8, 1954. I shall have occasion in the course of my remarks to refer to some of the information contained in these sessional papers, but I wanted to make it clear at the outset that my interest in this question is one of long standing.
I should like also to remind hon. members that this matter has been discussed in the Canadian House of Commons on quite a number of occasions. On most of those occasions the discussion has arisen out of some other matter, but on at least two occasions the matter was discussed on substantive motions. The first of those two occasions was in 1921, when Mr. A. R. McMaster introduced a bill to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act which was designed to have the same effect that my bill has at the present time. As that bill did not pass, I have not yet been able to find a copy of it, so I do not know whether my bill is exactly the same as that one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: It is not.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
At any rate the description of the bill which can be found in Hansard during the course of the discussion of the bill suggests that there is a striking similarity between Mr. McMaster's bill of 1921 and my bill of 1955. The second major debate on this matter was in 1922. Again it was Mr. McMaster who initiated the debate, but on that occasion it was on a private member's resolution rather than on a bill.
I invite hon. members to look at the debates of those two years of 1921 and 1922. They will find some very interesting reading. Hon. members will recall that in 1921 the Conservatives were in power and Mr. King was the leader of the Liberal opposition. Mr.. McMaster, who introduced the bill, was a Liberal and had played a very prominent part in the party; indeed I find he played a prominent part in the Liberal convention of
3980	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Senate and House of Commons Act
1919. He was very close to Mr. King, and I would point out that in 1921 he had Mr. King's support on his bill. That support was indicated by interjections by Mr. King in the debate and it was also indicated in a very concrete way by the vote which is recorded on page 665 of Hansard for March 8, 1921. It is always interesting to us who are now members of the House of Commons to look back over some of these ancient records and And there the names of great men of days gone by. Actually, the only person who is today a member of the House of Commons and who voted on that occasion is one whose name I am happy to mention, even though I do not agree with the way that he voted, because this gives me the opportunity to say how sorry all of us were to learn of the illness of the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mr. Casselman) and how pleased we have been to learn that he is making good progress. The hon. member for Grenville-Dundas was, as I say, the only present member who voted on that occasion. He happened to vote against the bill.
But one other member who is still a member of the house, although he did not record his vote on that occasion, was present, because he indicated that he was paired. In this instance I refer to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) who said he was paired with the then junior member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. R. H. Butts). The hon. member said that had he voted, he would have voted against the bill. In other words, the hon. member for Quebec South disagreed with Mr. McMaster, the sponsor of the bill, and he disagreed with his leader, Mr. Mackenzie King, on that occasion. Indeed it was not the only occasion when there was a difference of opinion between Mr. King and the hon. member for Quebec South. I find that Mr. Lapointe, the father of the present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe), and late minister of justice, was present on that occasion and along with Mr. King voted for this bill of Mr. McMaster's which would have had the effect of amending the Senate and House of Commons Act so as to prevent cabinet ministers from holding directorships in private firms.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: They were then in opposition.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Fort William is helping me out or anticipating what I am coming to. He says that they were then in opposition. He probably knows that when in 1922 these gentlemen crossed to the other side of the house they sang a different song. There is another name that interests me as I look over this list. I find that in 1921 there was a member for the

north riding of Oxford by the name of Mr. Nesbitt. He was a Conservative member of the House of Commons at that time, and he voted against the bill. That name suggested to me that there might be some relationship between him and the present member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). So I looked up the present Parliamentary Guide and I found that the present member for Oxford is a grandnephew of the Mr. Nesbitt who was the member for North Oxford in 1921. I hope the present member for Oxford will redeem the family name when the vote is called on this bill.
I invite members to look over this debate. As I say, it was introduced from the Liberal side of the house and very strong and cogent speeches were made by Mr. McMaster and others. Let me read one or two quotations from the speech of Mr. McMaster. I turn first of all to page 586 of Hansard of March 4, 1921:
I say that no man who is a minister of the Crown in this country has any time left to fulfil the duties of a director. That is my first proposition, and I think it is a proposition which will appeal as a reasonable one to members of this house. We have the best of authority for the statement that no man can serve two masters. Either he will have to neglect his duty as a minister or he will have to neglect his duty as a director, if he holds both positions at one and the same time.
On page 587 Mr. McMaster is recorded as having said:
Now, we should be, and I trust we all are, jealous for the good name of this House. We are told by authority, almost as great as the authority I have just quoted, that we are to "abstain from the very appearance of evil". Years ago Tennyson wrote about "the fierce light that beats upon the Throne".
Well, I do not think that light is comparable to the fierce light that beats upon men who enter parliament at this time of the world's history. I do not think that I am using the language of extravagance when I say that all governmental institutions are on trial and are being subjected to criticism which is not only strong but often bitter and often unjust.
That was not said yesterday, although it might have been. It was said 34 years ago by the sponsor of a bill similar to the one now before the house. I could go on with excerpts from the debate of March, 1921, but I will not take the time of the house to do so. I invite hon. members who are interested to get that volume of Hansard and read it. It is very interesting and very informative.
As the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) has invited me to inform the house, the next year the large number of Liberals who had voted for the bill when they were in opposition sang a different song when they were on the government side of the house. There was still one Liberal of course who

adhered to the principle that cabinet ministers should not be directors of private companies, namely Mr. McMaster, who himself introduced the resolution in 1922. It was a lengthy resolution.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: Was he the only one?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
The only Liberal who stuck by his guns? I am sorry, I have not yet taken the time to check all of the 59 who voted for Mr. McMaster's resolution in 1922 to determine whether any other of the 59 was a Liberal. Most of them appear to have been Progressives who had come into the house, together with men like Mr. Woods-worth and others. Mr. McMaster was amongst those who voted for the resolution in 1922. Mr. King and Mr. Lapointe voted against it that year. If I may offer this little bit to please the hon. member who has asked the question, I might say that the gentleman whose name I had occasion to mention yesterday was at least consistent. He voted against the proposition on both occasions. I refer to Arthur Meighen. He voted against the bill in 1921 and he voted against the resolution in 1922.
Mr. King had quite a time, as one would imagine, trying to explain why he took a different position in 1922 from that which he had taken in 1921. The gist of his argument was that he was now prime minister, that he now had about him some men in whom he had great confidence, and he just felt differently about the matter. After all, he even pleaded youth. He felt if he waited until he was an old man he might then tell the younger men in his cabinet what to do, but as long as he was just a young man that was not what he felt he should do. In fact, as found at page 1103 of Hansard for April 24, 1922, he said-

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: Were they to be the keepers of their own consciences just like today?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
I leave that for others to interpret, although I may come to it later. As reported at page 1103 of Hansard for April 24, 1922, Mr. King said:
There are times and places for everything. I have spoken of the Gladstone, the Campbell-Bannerman and, if you will, the Asquith tradition. May I remind my hon. friend that it was 1868 when Mr. Gladstone first became prime minister of England. He was then 59 years of age, and had had a long parliamentary experience. It was not until 1892, a quarter of a century afterwards, when he was past 80 years of age, that Mr. Gladstone sought to impose any self-denying ordinances upon his colleagues. If my hon. friend will give me time, and the occasion demands it, I shall be glad to follow the Gladstonian tradition.
That, Mr. Speaker, is just one quotation I have picked out from the interesting and
Senate and House of Commons Act much longer debate that took place in 1922 when, as I say, the resolution was defeated. I have already indicated it had the support of Mr. McMaster, the Liberal who had proposed the legislation the year before. It had the spoken support and the vote of my predecessor as the member for Winnipeg North Centre, Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, and the other Labour and Progressive members who were in the house. Some others among the 59 may have been Liberals or Conservatives. I have not been able to check all the names.
At any rate, Mr. Speaker, I think this does establish the point I made at the outset, that this is not an issue that has arisen to disturb the minds of public men or to disturb the writers of editorials in newspapers only in recent days or weeks. It is something that has been a cause for concern across a great many years, and I feel it is a matter of principle. I freely admit some things that have happened recently have brought the question out into the open and have attracted public interest to it, but I raise it as a matter of principle which I feel should concern the House of Commons.
Someone is going to say I am talking out my own bill. I regard the bill as too important to try to rush. There is more I want to say than can be said in the time remaining before six o'clock, so that in just a moment, Mr. Speaker, I shall be adjourning the debate. The next time we come to this matter I hope to have something to say about the practice followed in the United Kingdom. I shall make reference to something that happened recently in the United States. I shall also cite the Canadian practice in terms of what our prime ministers have done about the matter across the years, particularly from Sir Wilfrid Laurier's time to the present. I shall also deal with the arguments that have been advanced against my proposal such as the argument that it is something to be left to the conscience of individual ministers, and so on. That is a preview of what I will say when I get the chance to continue my remarks. In the meantime I hope all hon. members will recognize that this matter involves a very important principle, and I hope very serious attention will be given to it. On that basis, Mr. Speaker, I should like to move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Knowles the debate was adjourned.

speechtext: The interruption in my discussion has allowed me an opportunity, which normally I would not have had, Mr. Chairman, to rectify something in the early part of my speech. Evidently I have left the impression that miners are not working under arduous conditions these days, but that is not the impression I wanted to give to this house at all. I simply wanted to show that with the improvements in methods, material and equipment, and by extra effort a great showing was accruing to the industry. I did not want to create the impression that there have been only one or two improvements in the mining industry. The instance that I cited is general throughout the entire industry so that almost every type of employee working underground on production in the particular mine to which I referred receives pay ranging from an average of $20 per day to the $27 that I mentioned.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: You are talking about the metal mining industry.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: The base metal mining industry. Production has certainly increased. I believe it would be correct to say that, despite these improvements in income, the actual cost of production has not increased. A ton of ore is being produced just as cheaply today as it was 10 years ago.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
I have not as yet answered the question asked by the hon. member for Nanaimo. After answering that, I would be pleased to take another question from the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.
The hon. member for Nanaimo asked what had become of the miners who were displaced, and how many were displaced by these improvements in machinery and methods. As I said, I had not intended to make any contribution to this debate so I do not have the actual figures. However, for a few months each year I work in the mine and I am fairly well acquainted with what

has taken place. I would think that the actual labour force underground has been reduced by 75 to 100 men. This mechanization and improvement in methods has provided an opportunity for the mining company to work a very low grade of ore.
I am not a mining engineer, so I cannot say exactly what the savings have been. I know they are able to mine a very low grade ore and for that reason there has, been a certain measure of conservation. This has prolonged the life of a mine around which a large community has been built up and, in fact, up to very recently the community has been almost a single industry community.
In addition the same company, using these improved mining methods, has opened two additional mines. One I believe is producing up to 600 tons a day and the other one, which will be in production this year, will be producing around 500 tons. About 500 miners have been absorbed and employees from other areas have been engaged. At the Sullivan mine, where the original operations are located, a fertilizer industry has been introduced. A number of men from the mine have been re-employed, and I might say retrained, for the operation of the fertilizer plant. All in all, therefore, there has not been any grave dislocation of the men in the industry, and I can assure you that they are enjoying a considerably better standard of living. I appreciate the fact that it is not good enough, but as I said earlier I have no fear of improved methods and automation.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
Would the hon. member
permit my question now?

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: I was wondering if the hon. member would care to relate the purchasing power of the wage rates which he cited the miners as receiving today to the purchasing power of the $8 per day he cited them as having received a number of years ago?

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
Well, the hon. member's interjection has given me an opportunity to say again that this rate is the result of a contract system. The base rate would be $14 and some workers would go as high as $27 worked out between the company and union. Where the base rate is $13.59, the earnings go up as high as $20 per day. As to the value of the dollar compared with 15 or 20 years ago, I believe the hon. member is as well informed as anyone, and has probably done more research on the question because I understand he prepared himself for a speech on this question. I believe the generally accepted figure is about 50 cents on the dollar.
I said the original earnings were around $8 and if you double that they would be $16.

It is not every worker who would receive the $27, but there are people who are earning $27 per day. It is interesting to note that even during the time when the United States authorities seemed insistent upon a higher tariff on lead and zinc, there was no great concern. I feel that Consolidated would have survived that while some of the other companies would perhaps have gone under. There is no reason to believe that these improvements are not real. As I say, the hon. member can relate the actual value of the dollar as he wishes, but I would point out to him also that the miners are working a 40-hour week. They have more leisure time to spend fishing and so on and other pursuits.
However, I am being diverted from the point. I was going to say that the Minister of Labour should not be held entirely responsible for the unemployment we have today. There are many other factors, and the minister's job is more the finding of a solution, the administration of the labour code, unemployment insurance and so forth. However, in my view the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Finance have more important duties in maintaining balance in the economy.
Some hon. members have referred to the fact of the Prime Minister's stepping in at the time of the threatened railway strike in 1954, and have said that his efforts to bring the union and the railways together in an agreement reached the point of compulsory arbitration. They have also referred to the fact that at the time of the railway strike in 1950 the unions were forced to arbitrate with management in the settlement of their dispute.
I have some misgivings about the trend in this particular; but I think we must remember that employees in the transportation industry are in a different position from those who are working for industries in which prices and rates are allowed some measure of flexibility. When railway employees request wage increases, then whether we like it or not there arises the necessity for an adjustment in freight rates. Otherwise it seems almost impossible to increase wages. There is a measure of control by parliament over freight rates in Canada. Although that control is not completely rigid, when increases are authorized by the board of transport commissioners we hear a hue and cry in the House of Commons. For that reason freight rates are influenced by the action of parliament, and in this way there is not the same measure of flexibility in negotiations between railway employees and management. We should keep this
Supply-Labour
in mind, and try to work out some method of settlement of disputes so that there would be an understanding that, when necessary, rates would have to be increased.
Railway workers should not be expected to subsidize other industries as, in my opinion, they have done in the past. The hon. member for Prince Albert pointed out that high freight rates had caused a certain pulp company to which he referred to abandon plans to establish in northern Saskatchewan. Therefore high freight rates was one of the reasons for unemployment. However, the hon. member must know as well as anyone else that freight rates for export wheat from the prairies are set at a figure that was considered adequate in 1897, and the railways are still required to carry export wheat at those rates.
I have advocated a better way of providing for this discrepancy, by way of a subsidy paid by all Canada. To this point however I have not received much support. But when this very large amount of freight must be carried at a very low rate, some other commodify must pay the shot, with the result that freight rates make impossible the development of other new industries.
However, these are some of the conditions we must face. Simply to say in the House of Commons that freight rates are to blame for many of our difficulties, and simply to blame the minister for unemployment, is just not facing up to the facts.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that is all I have to say at the moment.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the debate on the first item of labour estimates has been somewhat long.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: Too long.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
There are some who think it has been too long, but I am not one who feels that way about it. I think the discussion has been well worth while, every bit of it-even the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace. Because while it was completely barren of ideas, and while the hon. member showed an utter bankruptcy of intellect with respect to matters we are facing, it did issue a challenge which ought to be taken up by hon. members who are trying to face these issues. Therefore I believe the debate has been exceedingly valuable.
In the course of the past two days a number of speeches have been made indicating just how seriously some members have been thinking, and how they have studied this matter. Also it seems to me some speeches have been given which show how completely at

Supply-Labour
sea so many members seem to be when faced with the challenging problems of today, particularly those related to unemployment and distribution.
I pause here for a moment to pay tribute to the Minister of Labour. Over the years, since I came to the House of Commons, and since he came as Minister of Labour, I have observed his work. I think he takes it seriously. 1 have never yet taken a problem to him without receiving his help, nor has there been any time when I have gone to him with a problem when he has not tried to find some equitable solution. Therefore I believe he is doing a good job in his department. I have nothing but sympathy and understanding for him in the work he is doing; and I do not think it is going to help him or anybody else to solve the problems of his department by simply trying to throw on him the blame for any situation -or, for that matter, on any one member of the government. Out of the sensible discussion that can and should take place in this forum of the people can come solutions, if we are ready to seek that which is right instead of standing here day after day and taking so much time to prove who is right or who is wrong.
Therefore I hope we will bear with the minister and try to give him some help. That is why I have felt like saying to him that I feel the discussion thus far has been good because a number of positive and forward looking proposals have been made. The members have asked him to give careful study and consideration to things which they hope will be solutions to the problems we face.
I have been interested in labour problems for many years. I might tell the minister that it was because I started studying problems relating to employment and recurring recessions that I was led into the Social Credit movement. I felt as I now feel that we had, if not a complete and full solution, certainly elements of solution which, if applied, will go a long way toward reaching a satisfactory solution. We are living in a most interesting and challenging time. We are living in a time, as has already been pointed out, of a rapid expansion of the use of automatic machinery in the productive enterprises. A good deal has been said about automation in this debate, not, I feel sure, in any way that would justify any reasonable member referring to it as a spread of gloom or blue ruin.
In his speech yesterday, the hon. member for Prince Albert, in referring to mechanization, said, not in exactly these words, but I think I got the sense of what he did say,
fMr. Low.]
that if any generation fears mechanization because they think that it will throw too many people out of work, the next generation finds that mechanization has tended to expand employment and to bring a higher standard of living. Well, that might be so, but I point out to him, and those who think as he does, that the second generation found that it was pretty slim going while the first one was passing away; and during the time that they were doing little or nothing to find a solution to the maladjustments that came as a consequence of mechanization, people- and my sympathies are with them-were the victims of, what shall I call it, a futile effort, if you want to call it that, or an attempt to find a satisfactory solution.
I am not for one moment saying that eventually we do not find a solution in answer to the problem, but I do not believe it is necessary to allow human suffering to continue as it has been allowed to continue over so many years at times in the past. If human ingenuity, brains and willingness to face facts were applied sensibly to the problems we would not have a lot of people suffer very long; they would not have to remain hungry very long in the midst of abundance; but- it is just that attitude, that everybody who puts forward an idea is a crackpot, that causes a continuation of human suffering. Anybody who disagrees with me and does not go along with the idea of laissez-faire is a crackpot. I am sorry to say that the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, who I am glad to see is in his seat tonight, feels that way. His whole talk this afternoon was nothing but that, and I am very sorry to see those ideas put forward in this day of all days when the lessons of economics and of human suffering should have borne in upon him, as on us all. What solutions are possible, and how should we set about to find them?
As I say, it might possibly be that the second generation after the one that fears mechanization might find a solution. But the second generations did discover, I am quite sure of that, in every case that they required an adjustment of thinking. It required new ideas and fresh approaches to social and economic behaviour and attitudes, and then changes for the better came.
The hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace says all you have to do is have faith. If that is all it takes to bring adjustments, then we should have had adjustments a long time ago, because we all have faith. We do not lack faith over here any more than you do. I just remind the hon. member that faith without works is dead. What we stand for is

faith with works, and intelligent works, at that, and a little bit of courage and vision and a little less of this silly business of calling other people crackpots because they come up with ideas. If you are going to discourage anybody who comes forward with a new idea by saying that he is imbued with the idea of funny money, well, for goodness' sake, how far are you going to get?
I heard the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace described this afternoon as an innocent abroad. Well, bless my soul, I hope there are not too many innocents abroad, if we are seriously and earnestly trying to find some way to cure the problem of unemployment. I am not going to indulge in namecalling because I do not think it helps; but he particularly engaged in ridicule and referred once or twice to the crackpots in this corner of the house.

speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT

speechtext: Yes, indeed.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: We should have a definition of "crackpot" to know whether it is parliamentary or not.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
Yes. I am not quibbling about it; it does not matter to me what it means at all. If by crackpot the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace and others like him mean someone who is really and seriously trying to find solutions to problems, I shall gladly take the name of crackpot.
The hon. member made special reference to my colleague, the hon. member for Bow River, and to what he said in this debate yesterday. He referred to him as a crepe-hanger and a crackpot. The hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace mentioned how senseless those arguments are about the results of the introduction of machines. Well, now, I took the trouble to look up what my colleague, the hon. member for Bow River, did say, and for the life of me I cannot understand how the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace reached the interpretation he did. I want to quote from page 3923 of Hansard, to show what the hon. member for Bow River did say:
I am not one who would suggest for a moment that we should decrease the use of machines in order to keep people at work. I do not think that is the purpose of civilization. I believe we should increase the use of the most technical machines to the point where, if the whole operation can be performed by pushing one button, so much the better.
I do not see anything to suggest crepehanging about that, or blue ruin. Bless my soul, that looks as though my hon. friend is not a bit afraid of mechanization or automation, as it has been so often referred to here.
Supply-Labour
The whole vein of my hon. friend's speech yesterday was like that. Therefore, I say it is hard for me to understand how the hon. member could possibly get from what the hon. member for Bow River said yesterday the interpretation that he tried to put upon it today; and yet my hon. friend did ridicule all of us in this corner, including the C.C.F. group. He called us crackpots, and he said that it would be swell if you have some funny money.
My hon. friend says that he has done some studying-perhaps he has. I would not deny that; but I shall take just a few moments to refer to the question of unemployment which we are discussing, and mechanization. I am going to take him back briefly through a little bit of history that he should have studied before he spoke this afternoon, because I think it will do him good to face facts which he did not face when he rose to his feet. Perhaps he did not think too much when he was on his feet today. Perhaps that is his trouble. Sometimes people's minds are so linked up that when they stand up the mind will not work. It is like that old steamboat that used to ply up and down the Mississippi in Lincoln's time. The stern wheel that drove it was so linked up with the whistle that when they blew the whistle the boat stopped. Compare that with the situation here.

speechtext: He may be a sternwheeler.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
