maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
That speech this afternoon was entirely a sternwheel speech. As I said, I should like to take the hon. member back through a little history which I am sure he would like to forget. I would like to refer for a few minutes to the labour and unemployment situation which existed during the Conservative regime of 1930-35. I am going to admit right off that in 1930 the Conservative government did inherit from the Liberal regime a very serious unemployment and recession problem.
There is no question about that. But they faced their responsibility with what policy? Just what was their policy? Was it automation? Was it progression? Was there a real effort to find a solution? I think I can describe their policy with regard to employment during the depression by saying that it was a case of push the steam shovel into the bush, bring out the wheelbarrows and shovels, put the unemployed into isolated camps and pay them 20 cents a day for digging a hole in one place and filling up a hole in another.

Supply-Labour
That was the kind of thing they offered to the people of Canada as a solution for the depression and unemployment problem. A serious situation developed over the years. The prices of primary products declined to a disastrous level and huge piles of products came into being. But many people who wanted those products found that they could not get them because they did not have purchasing power in their pockets and did not seem able to get any.
Every time anybody said to the Conservative government, "Why don't you get some purchasing power in circulation to start the wheels of industry going again?" the answer he got was, "There is not any money". They kept on saying that all through their regime up to 1935 when they were pitched out by the people of Canada largely because they had not found a solution or begun to find a solution for the unemployment problem.
The provinces tried in every way to persuade the Conservative government to do something to start the wheels of industry turning again so that salaries and wages would flow into the pockets of consumers. We felt that that was the answer. I was associated with a provincial government in those days and I know the problems we faced. I know how difficult it was to get the government down here moving on any project because the only answer we could get was, "There is no money". No matter how much we tried to show them how money could be obtained the answer always was that no money could be obtained.
I should like to refer to a specific instance and I do this for the edification of the hon. member from Montreal. I am not angry with him, not for a minute, but I think it would be a good thing to take his pants off and let him wander around here without them for a little while. I was living in Raymond in southern Alberta when the Conservative regime first came to power in 1930 and we went into the very serious part of the depression.
I was a teacher in the high school along with the hon. member for Lethbridge. We went through the whole of that year without having one five-cent piece by way of salary from our school board. I do not know just how we lived. There were plenty of goods and services but we could not get at them because we did not have money. We had to resort to a whole lot of things such as raising gardens, marketing eggs, borrowing milk from farmers and all that sort of thing. It is true we got along, and perhaps in some respects we were the healthiest, fattest and nakedest people in the world. But I want to tell you right 
now that it was tough going and I would not like to have to go through it again. I would not want my son to have to go through such a thing.
The school district could not pay our salaries because they discovered they owed the bank $67,000. They could not pay because they could not collect their taxes and the arrears of taxes had been hypothecated to the bank. Then the bank said, "No more". You could not blame them under the circumstances, but when they said "No more" we faced the problem of keeping the school running with 700 children and 18 or 20 teachers with no money available.
That was quite a problem but the people faced up to it and I think with some vision. I am wondering what the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace and his party would have done under the circumstances. Here is what we did. We realized that the goods and services were there in abundance in the community; we realized there were people willing to work, willing to apply their efforts to making more goods from the raw materials; prepared to give their efforts in distributing what was already in existence. We realized there were people prepared to teach the schools, to work for the city, to continue to give their services provided they could get goods in return. Willing workers and goods and services were available. The only thing that we needed was tickets of claim. Instead of sitting there wringing our hands, waiting for the next generation to solve the problem-

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: Like the Conservatives.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
-we had the faith of work. What did we do? We simply went to the town hall and had a chat with the mayor, the council and the secretary treasurer of the town who was a pretty forward-looking fellow. We said to him, "We will be prepared to continue teaching your school provided you will issue some tickets of your own; if you cannot get money at least you can provide some intermediary in the way of tickets or scrip."
They went to the Raymond Recorder and gave them a job of printing those tickets, which read, "The town of Raymond will pay to the bearer on demand $10 toward taxes, light rates or water rates." Those were handed out to us in payment for our services. We took them to the local storekeepers, the coal people and others, and said, "Will you accept these things in return for groceries and other things we need." They said, "What good are they?" "Well, you can take them to the town hall and pay your taxes with them; you can exchange them for your water rates; you can buy sugar with them from the sugar factory." We had arranged with the sugar

factory to accept them in payment for sugar and also with the coal men to accept them for coal.
When these storekeepers saw that it was possible to get these things they said, "Certainly, we will accept them." What happened? When they made a sale for one of these $20 or $10 pieces of scrip, quite often they had to make change in cash which began to dry up their scarce supply. So they went to the aluminum company and had them punch out aluminum disks saying, "We will pay to the bearer on demand 50 cents in groceries", or in hardware and so on. They passed those out. So with a pocket on one side filled with paper and a pocket on the other side filled with aluminum disks we walked the streets and were happy.
We even went so far as to establish foreign trade relations with Lethbridge twenty miles away. It was not very long until the stores, dealers and even the restaurants in Lethbridge and other places were accepting Raymond scrip because they knew they could exchange it for sugar from our town, for eggs, for butter and that sort of thing that came from the farmers in our district. They had no trouble over them. I remember the time when they gave me my first salary in over a year in this scrip. My wife and I went on a real tear. We went into the city of Lethbridge, 15 or 20 miles away, and proceeded to go to a picture show and go to the Greek restaurant for a meal-the first time we had been able to do such a horrible thing for well over a year. How joyful everyone was when goods began flowing in!
The upshot of it was that Raymond and district became a veritable oasis in an economic desert. All the teachers wanted to go to teach in Raymond because at least they were getting something with which to buy goods. This went on for several years. Let me first tell you that the only ones in the district who were not happy were the bankers, who sat in their offices and saw business bypass them and go to the town hall, which became the banker. All we did was recognize that the goods and services were there, that willing people were there and the consumers were there. The only thing that was not there was the tickets to claim those goods. We said that, if the country would not do something about it, this district would do something on its own and provide its own tickets. So tickets were distributed for services rendered and the goods were automatically distributed.
I cite that for my hon. friend and his colleagues who think as he does, to show them that it takes a good deal more than just faith to move goods, as it takes more than faith
50433-252J
Supply-Labour
to move mountains, but you will move mountains of goods if you use good sense as well as good faith. I would not advocate for one second that the same kind of process that was used in the town of Raymond be used in every community in Canada, but what I do point out to my hon. friend and his colleagues is this. The principle of what was done in the town of Raymond could have been applied on a national scale by the Conservative government with the same result that we had in the town of Raymond, but they did not have the imagination or the courage. They had the Bank of Canada, and they could have used it. The whole trouble was that they were going to sit there and let faith do the job, and faith just did not do it. As a consequence people suffered.
We have demonstrated without doubt that the ideas we put forward are not new and untried ideas; they are not crackpot ideas; they are ideas that have succeeded. Believe me-I point this out to my hon. friend- they have succeeded so well and we were getting along so beautifully in that district that a nurse in the city of Calgary, 170 miles away, a nurse we had never heard of, went to the courts and took out an injunction against the town of Raymond to prevent it from using its own form of purchasing power.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: Funny money.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
It was not the nurse who was interested in it. There were men who were hiding behind a woman's skirts, as they often do

people who saw in what we were doing a danger to their best vested interests. That is what was happening. As I said, it was only the bankers of the day who were unhappy about the situation. Yet, I say, a representative of a do-nothing party now stands up in this house and has the temerity to call the Social Credit group crepe-hanging prognosticators. Some of us have made a deep and realistic study in connection with the increasing use of automatic machinery to replace manpower in the chores of production. I am sure my hon. friend from Notre Dame de Grace will admit that the use of automatic machines does make it possible to produce things faster and cheaper than ever before. If he does not, he had better do some more reading, because that is the effect of it.
Now, what happens when, through the use of automation, things are produced faster and cheaper than ever before? It was that very question which I faced at university when I came face to face with the Social Credit solution. I was working on a project that had been given to me by the professor of economics at that school. This was the project. I saw some possibility through my

Supply-Labour
studies that the frequency of major depressions was accelerated by the increase in the speed with which things could be produced. So the professor suggested to me carrying on some studies in this respect. In the course of my studies I discovered this when I developed two graphs. One graph that I drew, based on exactly historical fact, indicated the space in years between major depressions. Then I superimposed upon that graph another one indicating the results of scientific studies with respect to the increase in percentage in the productive capacity of the economy through mechanization.
I was surprised, and so was my professor, to find that as the speed of production increased the time between major depressions in years declined almost exactly in inverse ratio, indicating that as we increase our speed of production we find it much more difficult to distribute the abundance that we can produce. I sought for and discovered this, which my hon. friend ought to discover in his reading: that the process of producing goods and services today, especially through the use of machinery, does not succeed in distributing salaries and wages, dividends and profits and compensation in all forms of purchasing power in sufficient quantities to enable the people to buy back what they have produced. As a consequence, gradually surpluses pile up, and when those surpluses have piled up to a certain point and big inventories have accumulated, the wheels of industry stop. When the wheels of industry stop people are thrown out of work, there are less salaries and wages to distribute, and as a result we fall into a depression. We do not get out of a depression until we take corrective action of some sort. Thus far, I point out to my hon. friend, the only way we have pulled out of major depressions in the past-that is, really major depressions- has been through war. That is the only way we got out of the depression of the thirties. We came out of it as a consequence of war and producing things for war purposes. During that wartime fully a third of all we produced, the top third, was skimmed off and sent abroad and given away as gifts to our enemies. We prayed that they would not send it back in the forms in which they wanted to send it. We also must remember that the purchasing power generated in producing those goods remained at home.
My hon. friend ought to take note of these things and do a little careful study.
Let me just point out briefly, in closing, something that my hon. friend should also have kept in mind. I have said a good deal about the period of the Conservative regime from 1930 to 1935, during which little or
[Mr. Low.l
nothing was done to haul us out of a depression. Now let me remind him of some of the things that have been done since. I have already pointed out that the war had done more than anything else to bring us out of the depression and restore purchasing power. I certainly decry the idea of waiting for wars to bring us out, but that is what will have to happen if we have many people with the mentality of my hon. friend from Notre Dame de Grace, because he will wait for the war.
We will never pull out any other way with his scheme of laissez faire. What else happened? What happened was that a very astute politician who used to sit across from us on this side of the house listened to this talk, listened to these ideas that were being put forward by those whom my hon. friend calls crackpots and said: There is something politically worth while in this. What did he do? He said: When these two million people who are now engaged in military effort come back and are rehabilitated into civil life and productive effort in Canada, what in the world are we going to do with all the production? We have not been able to any more than distribute what we have produced during the war without these two million.
He recognized that mechanization was going on apace, that automation was appearing, that the very things the hon. member spoke about this afternoon, automatic telephone exchanges and all that sort of thing, would soon be here in an increasing amount. So he said that something had to be done. How did he tackle the problem? He brought into being the family allowance program which has done a great deal to stabilize the economy and provide purchasing power to cover that part of production for which salaries, wages, dividends and profits just were not distributed and could not be distributed under our mechanized method of production.
He went further. He increased old age pensions to do a similar thing for people who had got beyond the years of productive effort. He also brought in increases in war veterans allowances and the like and, furthermore, developed what I think is one of the most balanced programs to look after unemployment that I know of, the unemployment insurance program of this government. All of that has served to distribute purchasing power to keep economic activity at a high level. But I point out to my hon. friend that, in spite of all these things, with the increasing rate of automation and the increasing displacement of manpower by automatic machines, in spite of the fact that we are spending billions for defence purposes to help

our neighbours and allies, in spite of all these things we have developed this year 600,000 unemployed.
Well, for goodness' sake, it is about time somebody woke up to the facts. That alone is an indication that automation is catching up on us, that we are in a period of serious dislocation, and that we are going to have to face this situation sooner than my hon. friend thinks. We are going to have to put our minds to this whole business and study ways and means of making a proper adjustment of purchasing power so that our people can continue to buy.
Let me point out to my hon. friend that machines do not get married and raise families. They do not have to have wages and salaries to keep going, and they can work for a fraction of a cent an hour where it takes $1 an hour at the very minimum for a man to keep body and soul together. It is about time we began looking at these things sensibly. I say to the hon. member that it is a dangerous thing for him or anybody else to stand up on the floor of the nation's forum and call people who have put forward positive ideas about how to meet these difficulties and adjust our dislocations, crackpots, funny money artists and all that sort of thing. They have no solution at all.
I think it is necessary for the Minister of Labour, his unemployment insurance commission, perhaps others in his employ, and certainly all of us in the house to give very careful study to what we can do to make proper adjustments in the economy consequent upon automation. In my judgment it is a question of adjustment and the maintenance of a free flow of purchasing power to keep economic activity at a high level. If the Conservatives ever do come to power with the same attitude as that portrayed by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace I predict that Canada will suffer the most tragic and intensive depression ever dreamed of by a frightened people.
But I say it need not be. It will be utter stupidity if it is allowed because depressions come about as the consequence of foolish policies of foolish men and can be cured and prevented by the positive policies of thinking men. Out of intelligent discussion of our problems solutions can be developed, but I say that no solution is to be found in silly ridicule or name-calling such as we had this afternoon. We have faith. We believe this country can slide into the golden age if we use our God-given brains to make the adjustments we ought to be making to meet the social and economic dislocations that occur through ever-increasing automation.
Supply-Labour

speechtext: He told us about what the Social Crediters did some years ago, but in view of the fact that in the province of British Columbia a former Conservative is premier, a former Conservative is finance minister-

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT

speechtext:
-and a former Conservative and director of one of the Canadian chartered banks is financial adviser, it seems rather strange that the speeches made by the hon. members to my left at that time are still being made at this stage in 1955 long after they have shed any Social Credit mantle they ever possessed. I will not pursue the

Supply-Labour
matter further at this point. My only comment regarding the speech made by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace is that, apart from being barren of ideas, I think it was typical of the attitude of mind of-and we should be thankful for it-a small segment of our population, the attitude that business can do no wrong, the old idea once expressed by Charles E. Wilson that what is good for General Motors is good for the United States. I think A1 Capp dealt the death blow to that in his comic strip. He had a character known as General Bullmoose who stated on quite a number of occasions, "What is good for General Bullmoose is good for everybody." I thought that when the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace was speaking this afternoon he took the attitude that whatever was good for business must of necessity be good for the workers and the farmers. Business was out to take care of the working people of this country; business was out to maintain high wages and so forth. I need make no further comment on that point.
During the course of this debate we have been treated to a number of lectures on history, and as a teacher of history I find it very difficult to resist the temptation to refer to one point of fact that perhaps elaborates the comments made the other day by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He referred to the labour difficulties in the city of Winnipeg, and to the fact that at that time a Conservative government, with indecent haste, passed a statute with the connivance and support of the Liberal opposition which had the effect of denying to Canadian citizens the fundamental rights which have always been considered to be part of the rights of British subjects. It was a government of the same party to which the hon. member for Prince Albert belongs. From time to time that hon. member has spoken in this house on the need for a bill of rights, and I agree with him 100 per cent. Certainly, however, the action taken by the Conservative government at that time would be in defiance of any bill of rights contemplated by any member of the house.
I can come closer to the present day with a little history. This morning I received a copy of the 128-page edition of the Regina Leader-Post, published of course in connection with our golden jubilee to be celebrated this year. In this special edition of the Leader-Post some of the history of Saskatchewan and the history of Regina is outlined. There is on page 10 of the third section a little bit of history in connection with an event which occurred in the city of Regina on July 1, 1935.

Hon. members will recall that under a Conservative regime the answer given to the single unemployed men was to put them away in relief camps, as they called them, for an indefinite period of time. In some cases it certainly went on for four years. The single unemployed men were expected to stay in enforced idleness, removed from their families and friends, taken out of the ordinary community life which I think all young Canadians would hope to enjoy, and with absolutely no hope for the future. These men, after being incarcerated in these relief camps or concentration camps for a period of time, decided that they wanted what we all believe to be the right of every Canadian, the right to work for a living. They took the only measure open to them and decided to come to the foot of the throne at Ottawa to lay before the government of this country their reasonable requests.
What were the requests of this group? The Regina Leader-Post story sums up the requests of the strikers at that time. There were six requests that they had to make of the Conservative government. The first was work at 50 cents an hour for unskilled men and at union rates for skilled men, for a five-day 30-hour week. In other words, they would work by the hour. They were anxious to spread the work around. It was not a question of making a great deal of money. All they asked was the establishment of a work and wages program to give them employment, even if it was a question of employing them on an hourly basis for only 30 hours per week. Then, they asked for compensation, social and unemployment insurance and the guarantee of their right to vote; recognition of the leaders of the strikers for negotiation purposes and an end of military control of relief camps.
No hon. member would suggest that these requests were unreasonable or out of line. When these men set out for Ottawa they got as far as Regina and, according to the bit of history in the Leader-Post, when the advance party arrived at Regina, they made a favourable impression. At that time the present Minister of Agriculture was the premier of Saskatchewan. These men made a good impression in the city of Regina, and when they came to the city every effort was made by the citizens of Regina to meet with them and to extend hospitality to them.
After a period of protracted negotiations the leaders of these single unemployed went to Ottawa to talk with the members of the Conservative cabinet. One newspaperman gives this report of an interview between one

member of the delegation and the late Prime Minister Bennett. Mr. Bennett is quoted as saying:
I ask you if you think you are playing the part of good citizens when you work against a country that is doing the best it can for you?
Now, there was an example of the attitude of the prime minister of Canada. Don't you fellows realize we are doing the best we possibly can for you? Ingrates coming to us and complaining! The thing is fantastic. These men were presenting their requests to the Conservative government at that time and they asked for a reasonable audience from the government. They were told by the Prime Minister that this country was doing all that it could, meaning the government was doing all it could, for them, and therefore they should be satisfied, be good citizens and go back to their relief camps where they should wait until the end of the depression. Here was the old idea that prosperity was just around the corner. If you waited long enough some day we might have a return to good times.
When the negotiations broke down, we know that on July 1-I am going to quote from the newspaper historical account-the following happened:
Then without warning steel helmeted police, mounties and Regina city police among them, moved in on the meeting at 8.20 o'clock. Five or six of the "strike leaders" were arrested and were being led away when some stones were thrown.
In other words they arrested a number of men who had previously announced in the city of Regina that they were ready for arrest at any time. As a matter of fact, they might have welcomed it in order that they might present their case before the courts. They would not have damaged their case by being arrested for the simple exercise of their right as citizens to request action from the government. We know that as a result of that riot one man was killed and over a hundred people were injured, most of them Regina citizens. Most of the relief camp strikers never left the Regina stadium where they were billeted. There were over a hundred injured and a great deal of property was damaged in the city of Regina. There is the story. When the single unemployed men in Canada asked for work and wages, the Tories gave them bullets and tear gas. Is it any wonder that the attitude of the people in my part of the country towards the Conservative party underwent a dramatic change? Our people will never forget the brutality and callousness of the last Conservative government in this country.
When I heard the Leader of the Opposition, the leader of the Conservative party in
Supply-Labour
Canada, get up and make some trips back into the history of this country to try to present the Conservative party as the friend of the workingman, I could not help but cast my mind back over those last days of the Conservative administration in this country from 1930 to 1935. Then, of course, according to Liberal spokesmen the depression was supposed to have ended in 1935. The other day in this house the hon. member for Vancouver South spoke of the great depression from 1930 to 1935. Let me tell him that there were over half the people of Saskatchewan on relief in 1936. Nothing the Liberals did at that time helped to bring about a solution of the unemployment problem. I mention this simply because the Leader of the Opposition has seen fit to go back into history to try to do the impossible, that is to try to portray the Conservative party as the friend of the workingman. A number of references along the same line were made by other speakers for the Conservative party. The hon. member for Greenwood the other day made an interjection with regard to the Winnipeg Labour trouble, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre answered, and I think rightly, by naming some of those people involved at that time, some of the people who were the most respected citizens in the city of Winnipeg. There was John Queen, who became mayor of that city, and Mr. J. S. Woodsworth who was perhaps the most respected man who ever sat in this House of Commons.
But I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Greenwood make some reference to those gentlemen in terms which indicated that they were communists of that time; I believe he said something to that effect.

I have here the number of people who were on relief in 1936, and there were 1,310,000 people on relief at that time. And yet the hon. member for Vancouver South seems to think that the depression was over, and that we had reached that corner around which prosperity was found.
I wish to make one reference to the remarks made the other day by the hon. member for Prince Albert. This is not the first occasion upon which he has made reference to the unemployment situation as it affects his province, and mine. In view of the fact that he has placed on the record two references to Saskatchewan which I think are inaccurate and misleading, to say the least, I wish to place a couple of figures on record, and to stress the fact that in Saskatchewan the problem of unemployment is related directly to farm income.
Saskatchewan is not an industrial province whatsoever. It is strictly an agricultural province. Secondary employment in Regina, for example, is related directly to farm income. I have received a communication from my own city regarding the unemployment situation there. I might say that the Trades and Labour Congress and the Regina labour council of the Canadian Congress of Labour in my city formed a joint committee to make a further investigation of the local situation, and they will be making a recommendation in due course. I wish to point out that in Canada as a whole we find that less than 14 per cent of those in the labour force are agricultural workers, whereas in Saskatchewan the reverse is true. There are not more than 25 per cent in the labour force of that agricultural province who could be classified as industrial, manufacturing or construction

workers. And to get that 25 per cent figure you have to add in a number of store employees.
So you find that essentially Saskatchewan is an agricultural community. You cannot possibly compare the unemployment picture, for example in the city of Regina, with that in an industrialized city like the city of Windsor. And of course it is utterly fantastic to draw a parallel of that kind.
At no time have I or any member of this group made any effort to attach blame to any one part of the country so far as unemployment is concerned. It is a national problem. Unemployment is something that affects the entire dominion. But I do wish to repeat and to stress once again that in Saskatchewan unemployment is related directly to falling farm income.
I know the hon. member for Prince Albert will agree with me when I say that unemployment in Saskatchewan is directly related to farm income. And farm income is one of those things over which the provincial government has very little if any control. In our province our farmers are engaged in the production of agricultural commodities for overseas markets. Very little of our wheat is consumed here; we are on the export market. Consequently the policy adopted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce will determine the condition of agriculture in Saskatchewan. And indirectly of course it affects the employment picture in my own city. I have the figures here-

It was not a point so much as it was a sort of inference; but the inference was sufficiently obvious that the hon. member for Temiscouata was able to get it right at the moment. He tried to convey the impression that the reason why there were so many unemployed in Saskatchewan was that the crown corporations have been laying off their employees, and these employees have been crowding the ranks of the recipients of unemployment insurance in that province.

In 1953 there were some 408,000 unplaced applicants at unemployment offices throughout Canada. At that time there were 3,700

employees of crown corporations in Saskatchewan. In 1955 the number of unplaced applicants in the national employment offices throughout Canada had risen to 632,913, as of March, 1955. With respect to the Department of Labour, I want to re-emphasize the comment made by an hon. member on the other side of the house a short while ago that the Minister of Labour is in a very unenviable position as Minister of Labour. In view of the very serious unemployment situation in Canada, it is only natural that the public mind would be thinking of the Minister of Labour as being the chief villain in the piece so far as unemployment is concerned.
Some hon. members have already pointed out that the Department of Labour does not possess the powers to deal effectively with the general question of unemployment. Unemployment is something which must be put on the doorstep of the Prime Minister and the entire cabinet. Certainly the Minister of Labour is not in a position in his own

department to deal effectively with a problem of that magnitude. Therefore, any criticism that we have made in respect to unemployment is certainly not levelled at the Minister of Labour. I am quite certain that the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance possess far more powers to deal with the general questions of unemployment and related economic problems than the minister of the labour department who is charged with very limited responsibilities in this connection. But I do want to refer to one question that was raised by my colleague, the hon. member for Cape Breton South, the other evening, and it is the only one I want to emphasize. I refer to the question of vocational training.
For some time we have been a little concerned about the future of vocational training in Canada. I believe questions have been asked in the house with respect to the future of the vocational training program, and the answers were not too satisfactory. It would appear that vocational training is not getting the proper consideration that it deserves from the government. At a time like this vocational training is of more importance than ever before.
A great deal has been said about automation and technological advances in general. As we approach closer and closer toward this perhaps ultimate goal of automation, there is less and less room in the labour force for unskilled labour. There might have been a time a few years back when a part of our labour force consisted of largely unskilled labour; but gradually the numbers of unskilled labourers required in our labour force have been diminishing and as our requirements of unskilled labour diminish it is all the more important to get skilled persons to take on the various jobs as they arise throughout the country.
We know that throughout Canada a great many of our young people are leaving school at an early age. Not too many of them are going on to college and university. These young people have to be equipped to take jobs in the increasingly greatly industrialized era that we are entering. It is not something that is just starting; it has been going on for a long period of time, but there is an acceleration of that tendency today. Certainly now is the time when we need greater emphasis on vocational training, not just for our young people. What about our older citizens, particularly those over 40 years of age?
Yesterday, my colleague, the hon. member for Cape Breton South, referred to the closing of 1-B colliery in Glace Bay, Nova Scotia. He pointed out that 60 per cent of the men

who were put out of employment in that mine were 40 years of age and over. What is going to happen to those men? Mining has been their life work. Certainly, employment opportunities have to be provided for them somehow or other. If a man has been brought up as a skilled craftsman in his own particular line of work and suddenly he is denied further access to that type of work, he has to be given the necessary opportunity to adapt himself to a new type of employment. Now is the time when we should be giving an increasing emphasis to vocational training, not only for our young people but for our older people, those people who are being displaced day by day through this whole process of automation.
It seems to me that the government has taken a retrograde step. I do not know the reason for it. Has the Minister of Finance something to do with it? Has he figured that he has to lop off expenses by cutting down vocational training grants? If so, it is a shortsighted policy.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make one or two comments upon the remarks made by the hon. member for Regina City. It seems to me that there ought to be certain decencies in the political life we are engaged in, and I think it is a poor piece of business, particularly for a teacher, to spend his time sneering at one of the great public servants who toiled for this country as few people have toiled. I refer to the man who was prime minister from 1930 to 1935.
Let us be honest and admit that the period from 1930 to 1935 was a time when not only did world trade dry up but western Canada dried up. I was in business during those years and it was my duty to go to western Canada and I saw things there during the drought that I never thought possible. I saw sights that reminded me of what I imagined the Sahara desert looked like. But for people to come along now and criticize the men of those days, overlooking the situation as it existed then, and overlooking that we have new financial tools-we have the Bank of Canada which was set up by the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett-is not good business.

Supply-Labour
why I rose to my feet because I considered R. B. Bennett to be a great citizen who served this country in times of incredible difficulties and it is a poor piece of business to be trying to diminish his reputation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: Is the minister not going to answer some of the many questions?

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have followed this far-flung discussion yesterday and today and have made a great many notes. I think it would add to the orderliness of the discussion if I were to state that as we reach the particular items in my estimates I shall do my utmost to answer the questions and comments and criticisms that have been made with regard to those items. I would make one reservation in that I did promise that I would reply to a criticism made before dinner by the hon. member for Winnipeg North. I would like to do that. If we do not reach the fair employment practices item, which is only the third or fourth item, before 9.58 o'clock I shall answer his comment then.

Item agreed to.
175. Annuities Act-administration, $1,015,522.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have had some correspondence recently in connection with annuities. The trouble seems to be that there is no cash surrender provision in connection with annuities. I think it was 1951 when the government introduced a bill containing a cash surrender clause. I am sure the minister must remember this. As I say, if a man takes out an annuity he cannot possibly get his money back. This is what the department tells me.
I should like to ask the minister if the government has any intention in the near future of amending the annuities act so that under extenuating circumstances the annuitant would be able to get back his money. In the case I have in mind a man has lost his car and is forced to sell some of his household effects. He has an annuity but he cannot touch it. Perhaps the minister can answer me now, or even later. Apparently the bill that the government brought down before to which I have referred was dropped by the wayside somewhere.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: It is not the intention of the government, at this session at any rate, to bring in an amendment to make the equity in an annuity refundable. The whole act has had consideration, but the particular provision just suggested would seem to be out of harmony with the original intention of the annuity plan which was to encourage thrift for old age.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: When the supplementary estimates were up for consideration in March they contained an item of $26,000 on which very little explanation was given. I believe I intimated to the committee at that time that when the main item came up I would ask some questions about it. If my memory serves me well, I asked what that $26,000 was for and was told that additional commissions had had to be paid because of additional sales of annuities which had not been anticipated by the department. At that time, again I am trusting to my memory, the Minister of Finance agreed with that statement. Despite that and the fact that I gained the impression that he expected this picture to continue and that there would be more annuities sold this year than there were last year, I find the same amount in the estimates appropriated for commission to agents as there was in the estimates for last year, that is $270,000. I should like to know just what the situation really is. If the trend is towards greater and greater sales, that is poor budgeting. If, on the other hand, it was a once-in-a-lifetime sale, I would be interested to know just what it was that caused the additional expenditure of $26,000. Was it a general increase in business, was it industrial coverage for a large number of people, or just what did occasion that $26,000 additional appropriation?

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the explanation given in regard to the supplementary estimates was correct, that the sales that were made last year had accrued commissions for which we did not have enough money. Perhaps my hon. friend would permit me later on to refer more definitely to her inquiry with regard to comparing the amount set out for commissions this year, $270,000, with the $296,000 for last year. I should be glad to do that.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: I asked this question of the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Labour not being in the house at the time this item was passed. He did not have the information at his fingertips. I intimated that I intended to ask the Minister of Labour whether this was a general increase; was it one large coverage that was sold, or just what did occasion that amount of $26,000? I am sure the minister follows me. If there was a general increase in business, why is that amount not appropriated for this year also? If the sale of annuities is becoming so popular and the agents so active that they are gradually increasing business, then why is an increased amount not in the estimates this year?

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: That is the point I should like to make sure about. I can say that the increased amount of commission asked for in the supplementary estimates was due to a general increase in business last year. I cannot for the moment say why we were a little pessimistic about future business in making up what is here our main estimates for this year.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: I understand that there are two groups of agents, ordinary salesmen and postmasters.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: Our sales force is pretty steady.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: I notice also that in this department, quite apart from the commission, last year there was an expenditure of $1,009,597, as against an appropriation of $997,528. I suppose that the increase of $26,000 would be included in that. Despite that, the appropriation for this year is even another $6,000 higher than the expenditure. It is hard to reconcile these figures without taking out the $26,000. You really have to add the $26,000 to the original appropriation of last year, and you get $1,023,000. The estimated expenditure is $1,009,000. I do not want to pin the minister down at this time of night to a full statement on expenditures, but I rather think that if we got to the bottom of the $26,000 we would get an idea of what the rest of it is about.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
I too do not wish to hold up these estimates at this time of night but I do want, for the third consecutive year, to object to this expenditure. In my opinion it simply cannot be justified. During 1955 the government is proposing to spend $1,015,000 on the administrative costs of annuities. I think it is worth while noting that such an amount is about $18,000 more than last year. I think hon. members, as they look at this expenditure, should keep in mind the original purpose of this annuities legislation. The original Government Annuities Act was passed in 1908. The reason it was passed was to help people of moderate means to put away money for their old age. Since that time of course old age pension legislation has been passed. Despite that fact I still think there is a place in our over-all social security system for annuities. As a matter of fact, I am one who thinks that probably the ceiling should be increased from $1,200 to $2,400. At the same time, I feel very strongly that this annuities department should be placed on a self-sufficient basis. There is no earthly reason why the taxpayers of Canada should be subsidizing these annuities. It is worth
Supply-Labour
while noting that, in addition to this administrative item, the government is paying out a substantial sum each year to keep the fund on a sound basis. During 1955, I believe, it is about $250,000. In past years the sum has been considerably higher.
That means that this year the taxpayer of Canada is subsidizing the annuities branch, or to be more exact, those who hold annuities, to the extent of $1,265,000. Since this legislation originated, the over-all subsidy now totals more than $32 million. Now, I contend, as I have contended in the past, that government policy in this respect should be changed. I am all in favour of government annuities being sold at cost; I think that is sensible. I do not think the government should try to sell these annuities at a profit. But I certainly do not think that the government should continue to sell annuities at a loss.
If such a policy were followed the annuities branch could still sell these annuities at less than insurance companies could sell similar policies. I take this attitude tonight particularly because so few people are benefiting from this subsidy. Last year a total of 18,466 individual and group contracts were issued. That means, in other words, that the taxpayer of Canada subsidized each and every contract, for administrative costs alone, to the extent of $54. As I see it, the Minister of Labour, and the Minister of Finance, should give serious consideration to changing government policy, so that these annuities are sold at a price which is sufficient, first of all, to cover administrative costs, and secondly, to keep the fund solvent.
I can see no reason whatever why the taxpayer of Canada should be called upon to subsidize a scheme which is used by only a small minority of our population, most of whom are in no need of such government assistance. Moreover, I see no reason why the government must employ 174 people at the taxpayers' expense, simply to sell an article at below cost and in competition with existing companies. Today it is not always- indeed, very frequently it is not-people in low income groups who buy annuities. Quite often it is people who are in the higher wage category who buy the annuities.
Many people say that the cost of government should be brought down. If hon. members believe that fact, I suggest that this is a good place where they could start trimming. Therefore I move:
That item 175, on page 31 of the estimates, which calls for an expenditure of $1,015,522, be reduced to the sum of $1.
If I need a seconder, the hon. member for Chicoutimi will second this motion.

Party solidarity.

Supply-Labour

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: I should like to say a word or two about the amendment now before the committee. First of all, may I say that I do not hold any annuities. I have never been able to buy any, but I can see the advantage of having them. I would agree with the mover of the amendment to the extent of saying that the department, particularly the annuities branch, is overmanned. I think some economy could be practised in that regard and maybe they could save enough money to balance the accounts. But I do not think it would be a good thing to do away with the government annuities branch. I maintain this is one instance where the ordinary working individual has an opportunity to make an investment which gives him a fair and decent return.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: I think so too.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre says he agrees with that.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: Just make it self-sufficient.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
It seems to me that to give the ordinary little man a place to invest his money so that he can draw a fair amount of interest on it and have some security is a worth-while thing to do. It is the sort of investment that is not available to him from any private organization I know of at that rate of interest. I have investigated the matter with the insurance companies and I find that what they have to offer cannot compare with government annuities.
I want to take exception to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Selkirk. I would be very sorry indeed to see any cash surrender clause provided in the annuities legislation whereby the money could be withdrawn. To me that is a safeguard to be retained. I do not think any person who has worked hard to save enough money to invest in an annuity so that he can have some form of benefit in his later years should be allowed because of financial stress or simply because he wishes to do so to withdraw that money and then live in poverty after that. I can understand the hon. member's concern. There might be an elderly person who had a doctor bill that should be paid, but I would be the last one in the world to say that they should cash in their annuity in order to pay a doctor bill, much as I would like to see them pay it. My experience is that the doctors probably can get along a little bit better than the person who is in such need that they want to cash their annuity in order to pay the bill. Then they would not have the benefit of a monthly annuity payment to assist them in their old age.

No, Mr. Chairman, I would not sanction a cash surrender provision being put into the annuity legislation. I think it should be left exactly as it is. If a person has an ordinary straight annuity they should be protected against all claims so that they will be able to draw their monthly cheque to assist them in their time of need and be able to make use of the assistance which they worked so hard to provide.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: Possibly I should not even speak on this particular subject because I happen to possess one of the annuities which I took out in the year 1928. In view of what has happened in Alberta in the last three or four weeks it may be I am disqualified from sitting in the house because I have one of these annuities. I am not too sure of my position from that point of view. My main reason for rising was to ask, with reference to the very considerable amount of $475,177 estimated for this year for staff wages, and being part of the total of $1,600,000 odd, whether it is all charged against the general annuities scheme or whether it is a straight contribution by the people of Canada towards the plan.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: It is a straight contribution of the taxpayers towards the annuities plan. I should like to refer to the question of the hon. member for Hamilton West. In both cases, for 1954-55 and for 1955-56, the answer is that it was a case of underestimating at the time the main estimates were prepared. We are called upon in October to make up our estimates, and at that time it was not clear how much would be needed for commissions. We asked for $26,000 more last year, and I have to tell the Minister of Finance that we will be asking for $35,000 in the supplementary estimates this year. If I have permission, I should like to refer, before ten o'clock is called, to the very special question raised this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North. He charged that the government is violating the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. He based his charge on a document which he held in his hand and which he indicated called for certain information that was contrary to the spirit and the letter of the act. I should like to tell him and the house that the unemployment policy of the government is of course conducted by the civil service commission-the employment policy, I mean. I have heard so much about unemployment!

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext: The truth will out.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
The carrying out of the policy of the federal government in employing staff

is the task of the civil service commission, and the commission does attempt to carry out fully the letter and the spirit of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. Needless to say, the government believes that should be done.
The hon. member kindly sent me the document he had in his hand this afternoon, and I was glad to see that it was not an application for employment in the civil service at all but rather a confidential questionnaire used for security purposes only. It is used in connection with personnel occupying vulnerable posts so far as security is concerned. I am told that only with persons holding or applying for posts that may give access to vital information or some other similar matter is this form used.
In view of what I have said, I hardly think its use in this way is contrary to section 11 of the act which reads as follows:
Nothing in this act shall be construed to require a person to employ anyone or to do or refrain from doing any other thing contrary to any instruction, direction or regulation given or made by or on behalf of the government of Canada in the interests of the safety or security of Canada or any state allied or associated with Canada.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF CABINET MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I must take issue with the minister on this subject. In the first place, the act deals with something more than with forms of application for employment. The act states in subsection 5 of section 4:
No person shall . . . make any written . . . inquiry in connection with employment that expresses either directly or indirectly any limitation. specification or preference as to race . . .
And so on. This is a written inquiry. It certainly is not a questionnaire concerning employment. It is a written inquiry, and the minister tells me now that this inquiry is only used in those tender, soft spots where security may be at stake. But how is the security of Canada safeguarded by finding out what a civil servant's father's nationality was? How is the security of the state furthered by finding out the nationality of the dead parent of a civil servant? I may say I did not get this document from the person who received it originally from whatever branch of the government it was he was in. I got it from an intermediary. I am informed on what I consider to be good authority that the position this person was seeking was as sensitive as that of member of parliament, and members of parliament are not allowed to know too much.
I am quite certain that despite the belief of the minister this form has been used in other departments of government. I have no objection at all to the most stringent security
Supply-Labour
regulations. After all, they are necessary. I cannot imagine, from the point of view of security and protecting Canada against possible treachery-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
On Monday we shall take the committee of the whole on Bill No. 188, the Government Employees Compensation Act, committee of the whole on Bill No. 279, the great lakes fisheries convention; the second reading of Bill No. 351 respecting Canadian National Railways; second reading of Bill No. 352 respecting the inspection of meat and meat products; the resolution stage of the bill with respect to national standards for agricultural products; the resolution with respect to the Yukon Quartz Mining Act; the second reading of Bill No. 5 to amend the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act; the second reading of Bill No. 350 to amend the Blind Persons Act.
If I might have the indulgence of the house for just one moment, I would ask the serious consideration of all members to the business of the house for the next few weeks. We had all, I think, hoped earlier, if I may say so, that we might conclude the session some

Supply-Labour
time about the middle of June. I should like to point out that there are six or seven committees still functioning and meeting two and in some cases three times a day. It would be desirable to get the committee work cleaned up, I would hope, during the course of the next week, if at all possible, so that very shortly after that it would be possible to meet in the mornings in the house.
What I say now is not by way of criticism at all of anyone or any group, but often we find, sir, that in the last two weeks we have to do more contraction perhaps of what members would like to say and do than should be necessary if we started a little rationing a little earlier. I should like to point out that in this particular debate on labour we took almost nine hours, I think about eight and three-quarter hours, to carry the first item. We took a little over three hours to carry the first item last year, and I do not think there is any particular reason for that. We had a long unemployment debate in both sessions, so I just appeal to hon. members to bear in mind that if we would have the time to give full consideration to all the business that is going to come before parliament we might consider, beginning on Monday, endeavouring to find a way to state party positions and individual positions with perhaps a little less debate than we have had.

If I could comment on the minister's remarks and his reference to the fact that the debate on the first item of labour estimates last year took but three hours, I would remind him that it was about the next to the last day of the session and
the whole thing was considered very quickly with the co-operation of both sides of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is my point. If, beginning on Monday, we would state our positions of course on all legislation and on all estimates, but nevertheless keeping debate down to a minimum, we would not have to contract an important debate in the last week.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question? Will the business on Tuesday be a continuation of that which is not concluded on Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I hope we will take the remainder of the legislation on the order paper, having disposed of all that I mentioned for Monday.
May I ask the minister what he intends to do about setting up the committee on atomic energy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
